Interpreting the OPG

  • The OPG is a tomographic radiograph whose focal trough approximates the curve of the mandible. Posterior parts of the image are lateral views; the anterior part is an anterior–posterior view.
  • Limits: lower resolution than intra-orals, many superimpositions (especially sinus and palate), distortion, ghost shadows, and no medial–lateral information → CT, CBCT or MRI.
  • Perschbacher: osseous structures and soft tissues first (starting at the periphery) → alveolar processes → teeth last.
  • Cosson: count the teeth → mandible right to left → maxillary sinuses → peripheries.
  • Dose ≈0.014 mSv (chest X-ray 0.02 mSv) · fractures: angle 32%, second fracture at the parasymphysis in 40% · OKCT recurrence up to 62%.
Paper 1 · Perschbacher 2012 · educational review

Interpretation of panoramic radiographs

Aust Dent J 2012;57(1 Suppl):40–45 · Department of Radiology, University of Toronto

The OPG is a complex projection with multiple superimpositions and distortions, made worse by technical errors, and it shows many structures outside the jaws. Interpretation starts with knowing normal head and neck anatomy and how it appears on this image.

Panoramic perspective and osseous anatomy

  • The X-ray tube rotates around the head, so the perspective changes: the right and left posterior parts are lateral views; the anterior part is an anterior–posterior view. The image is like a composite of two lateral and one AP skull view, with fewer superimpositions.
  • Pterygoid plates + posterior maxilla → pterygomaxillary fissures. Zygomatic processes of the maxilla → J-shaped shadows over the sinuses. Zygomatic arches → temporal bone (upper part of the TMJ).
  • Mastoid processes (air cells) are sometimes imaged behind and below the TMJ. Mastoid air cells may pneumatise the roof of the TMJ — a normal variant that can mimic multilocular pathology (Fig 2).
  • Lateral and inferior orbital rims; infraorbital canal (thin parallel cortices); inferior turbinates cast surprisingly large shadows across the sinuses; the hyoid can superimpose on the inferior border of the mandible depending on positioning.

Soft tissues and air spaces

  • Soft tissues: external nose over the maxillary incisor apices; external ear over the condyle, earlobe as a rounded opacity behind the ramus; tongue — the largest intra-oral shadow (dome-shaped), irregular posteriorly from the lingual tonsils; epiglottis — a finger-like projection below the angles of the mandible; soft palate — oval or inverted tear-drop shape off the hard palate.
  • Air spaces (nasal fossa, nasopharynx, oropharynx, oral cavity, oral orifice) are radiolucent and can be mistaken for bone-destroying pathology or fractures.
  • Oral cavity (gap between tongue and palate): overexposure can obscure the roots of the anterior teeth → have the patient place the tongue flat against the palate.
  • Oral orifice: a "kiss-shaped" radiolucency over the incisor crowns → close the lips around the bite-stick.

Ghost shadows

Structures imaged outside the focal trough appear magnified and blurred.

  • Contralateral mandible: the beam passes through the opposite side, so its ghost appears slightly superior, reversed, enlarged and indistinct.
  • Cervical spine: in focus at the posterior edges; its ghost obscures the anterior jaws because the beam originates behind the head → patient stands as tall as possible with the C-spine maximally extended.
  • Earrings and facial jewellery: remove them — the right earring projected over the left maxillary sinus and the left earring over the right zygomatic arch (Fig 6).

Systematic approach

"An observer cannot count on abnormalities to present themselves." Assess the osseous structures and surrounding soft tissues first, then the alveolar processes, and the teeth last. Bilateral findings are generally anatomic; asymmetry may indicate disease or a developmental condition.

  1. Periphery and corners — start here to avoid zoning in on the teeth: orbits, articular processes (TMJ), cervical spine, styloid processes, pharynx, hyoid.
  2. Outer cortices of the mandible — one circuit: anterior and posterior rami, coronoid processes, condyles and necks, inferior border; look for continuity and evenness.
  3. Cortices of the maxilla — posterior and medial walls and floor of each sinus. With the posterior wall, also check the zygomatic process of the maxilla and the pterygomaxillary fissure: three roughly parallel lines. Erosion of the posterior wall is easily missed unless all three are identified (Fig 8).
  4. Zygomatic bones and arches, back to the temporal bones.
  5. Internal density of the maxillary sinuses (left vs right) — opacification is most commonly inflammatory but could be more serious.
  6. Nasal cavity and palates — nasal floor/hard palate, conchae, septum, soft palate into the oropharynx.
  7. Bone pattern — trabecular density and pattern (some metabolic conditions alter it generally, so left–right comparison may not help); IAN canals, mandibular and mental foramina (size, position, cortication, symmetry).

Alveolar processes and teeth (resolution much lower than intra-orals): work clockwise from posterior Q1 to posterior Q4, repeating the sweep for each finding — (1) crestal bone (periodontal bone loss); (2) PDL spaces and lamina dura (inflammatory disease); (3) follicles and papillae of developing teeth; (4) the teeth — presence, eruption/position, caries, inadequate restorations, calculus, developmental or acquired abnormalities.

Pathology and limits

  • Especially useful for regions intra-orals can't image: TMJs (overview only — rules out major abnormality) and third-molar regions.
  • Shows a lesion's entire boundary: location, periphery and shape, internal density, effects on surrounding structures.
  • Limited by superimpositions (especially maxillary sinus and palate) and inability to show medial–lateral changes → CT, CBCT or MRI.
Paper 2 · Cosson 2020 · clinical review for GPs

Interpreting an orthopantomogram

Aust J Gen Pract 2020;49(9):550–555 · OMFS surgeon · commissioned, externally peer reviewed
  • A tomographic extra-oral radiograph with a focal trough approximating the curve of the mandible. Less detailed than intra-orals, but shows gross changes in calcification (caries) and ossification (periodontal bone loss, abscess, cyst). The flattened curve has to be reinterpreted mentally in 3D.
  • Often ordered by dentists as a screening tool. Dose ≈0.014 mSv vs 0.02 mSv for a chest X-ray. Being extra-oral, it works with limited opening or a strong gag reflex.
  • Artefacts: patient movement (the tube head and detector circle the head); the bite block records the mandible protrusive, so the condylar head sits anterior to its rest position in the glenoid fossa; the C-spine may obscure the anterior teeth; the occipital bone may project over the opposite rami; a lead apron can cause an anterior artefact (Fig 1).
  1. Count all teeth and positions; note missing or misplaced teeth.
  2. Follow the mandible from right (image left) to left: condylar head size/shape, continuity of the ramus and body border, uniform internal density, IAN canal ending at the mental foramina.
  3. Maxillary sinuses: opacities or lucencies; cortical outline continuity.
  4. Peripheries: cervical spine, zygomatic, submandibular or hyoid abnormalities.

FDI numbering: quadrant first, then tooth (e.g. 48). Deciduous teeth are 1–5 in quadrants 5–8, or occasionally A–E.

Pathology

  • Caries: demineralisation of enamel and dentine by organic acids from oral bacteria. An infected, necrotic pulp → abscess → radiolucency under the roots.
  • Third-molar impactions (a common reason for an OPG) are classified by the angle of impaction (Fig 10).
  • Edentulous atrophy: alveolar bone is lost, then basal bone. When severe → pathological fracture ("bucket-handle", Fig 12; treatment difficult because of low bone stock) and IAN neurosensory change.
  • Radiolucent lesions: odontogenic cysts, infective, developmental, or less commonly metastases or metabolic conditions. Cyst — well-defined, often asymptomatic, may or may not contact teeth. Abscess — usually painful, always in contact with the associated tooth. All odontogenic cysts are benign but need removal (bone destruction, infection).
  • Locally aggressive lesions such as the OKCT and ameloblastoma can only be differentiated from other lesions by biopsy → refer. A dentigerous cyst displacing 48 inferiorly can look like an OKCT — only histology of the lining tells them apart. OKCT recurrence is up to 62% → radiographic follow-up for life.
  • A maxillary cystic lesion with internal calcification around an impacted molar (mixed dentition) proved to be a complex odontoma at enucleation.

Trauma

  • Useful especially for the mandible; read with emphasis on cortical continuity. Facial-bone fractures often need further plain views or CT (overlap, angulation).
  • Commonest site: the angle (32%); a second fracture at the parasymphysis occurs in 40% of patients (Dongas & Hall 2002).
  • Cortical overlap → a second, perpendicular (PA) view.
  • Dislocation: both condylar heads anterior to the articular eminences (Fig 17); reduction sometimes needs sedation or anaesthesia.

Conclusion: a useful screening radiograph of the dentition and facial skeleton, commonly ordered for third molars and a baseline for new patients; read it systematically with knowledge of the anatomy.

Compare & contrast
Perschbacher 2012Cosson 2020
Author / audienceOral radiologist; dental readershipOMFS surgeon; general practitioners
Reading orderPeriphery and bone first, teeth lastTeeth first, periphery last
EmphasisImage formation: perspective, air spaces, ghost shadows, the three posterior-maxilla linesClinical use: dose, numbering, impactions, cysts vs abscess, fractures, dislocation
Agree onA systematic approach and knowledge of anatomy; the OPG is an overview with lower resolution than intra-orals; further imaging when needed.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Clear teaching papers illustrated with labelled radiographs.
  • Perschbacher explains why artefacts arise, so they can be prevented at exposure.
  • Cosson links findings to action: referral, biopsy, extra views, follow-up.
Limitations
  • Single-author narrative reviews — expert opinion, no diagnostic-accuracy data.
  • Neither shows that its reading order reduces missed findings.
  • Perschbacher doesn't cover dose or indications; Cosson's short method omits ghost shadows and a tooth-by-tooth alveolar sweep.
Clinical relevance
  • Use one routine on every OPG, including the corners (TMJs, styloids, sinuses, hyoid, C-spine).
  • Prevent artefacts at exposure: tongue to palate, lips closed on the bite-stick, patient standing tall, jewellery removed.
  • Know when the OPG isn't enough: intra-orals for detail, a PA view for overlapping fractures, CT/CBCT/MRI for medial–lateral extent, biopsy and referral for suspicious lesions.
Exam practice
SAQExplain the "panoramic perspective".

The tube rotates around the head, so the right and left posterior parts of the image are lateral views and the anterior part is an anterior–posterior view — like a composite of two lateral and one AP skull view, with fewer superimpositions.

SAQWhat is a ghost shadow? Give three examples and how each is managed.

The image of a structure outside the focal trough — magnified and blurred. Contralateral mandible (slightly superior, reversed) — recognise it. Cervical spine over the anterior jaws — patient stands tall with the neck extended. Earrings/jewellery projected on the opposite side — remove them.

SAQList Cosson's four steps and contrast them with Perschbacher's order.

(1) Count the teeth; (2) trace the mandible right to left, including the IAN canal; (3) maxillary sinuses; (4) peripheries. Perschbacher reverses the emphasis: periphery and osseous structures first, teeth last, to avoid zoning in on the teeth and missing findings around the jaws.

SAQName two air-space artefacts caused by patient positioning and how to prevent them.

The tongue–palate air space (overexposure obscures the anterior roots; may mimic a fracture over the ramus) → tongue flat against the palate. The "kiss-shaped" oral orifice over the incisor crowns → close the lips around the bite-stick.

SAQHow does a cyst differ from an abscess on an OPG, and why refer some radiolucent lesions?

Cyst: well-defined, often asymptomatic, may or may not contact teeth. Abscess: usually painful, always in contact with the associated tooth. OKCTs and ameloblastomas can only be differentiated by biopsy → referral; OKCTs recur in up to 62%, so lifelong radiographic follow-up.

SAQWhat is the commonest mandibular fracture site, and what should you do next?

The angle (32%). Look for a second fracture — at the parasymphysis in 40% of patients. Check cortical continuity; if cortices overlap, take a perpendicular (PA) view.

LAQDescribe a systematic approach to interpreting an OPG and discuss its strengths, limitations and when further imaging is needed.
  1. The image: tomographic, focal trough; lateral posterior and AP anterior perspective; low dose (≈0.014 mSv); extra-oral (limited opening, gag reflex).
  2. Before reading: normal anatomy, air spaces, ghost shadows; prevent artefacts at exposure (tongue, lips, posture, jewellery, bite block).
  3. Approach: Perschbacher's 7 steps from the periphery, then alveolar bone and teeth clockwise Q1→Q4 for each finding; contrast with Cosson's 4 steps. Compare left and right.
  4. Strengths and limits: whole-jaw overview, TMJs, third molars, lesion boundaries, trauma screening vs lower resolution, superimposition, distortion, ghosting, no medial–lateral dimension.
  5. Further imaging: intra-orals for detail; PA view for overlapping fractures; CT/CBCT/MRI for medial–lateral extent; biopsy for OKCT/ameloblastoma. Both papers are expert opinion without accuracy data — consistency matters most.

CAMBRA — caries management by risk assessment

  • CAMBRA is a concept, not a product or a form: (i) assess risk, (ii) reduce pathological factors, (iii) enhance protective factors, (iv) minimally invasive restorative care.
  • Caries balance: disease indicators WREC + risk factors BAD vs protective factors SAFER. Any one WREC indicator = high risk. Extreme = high + hyposalivation.
  • Validation (2011): new cavitation at follow-up in 24% low · ≈40% moderate · close to 70% high · 88% extreme.
  • RCT: CHX + fluoride → 24% lower 2-year increment in high-risk adults; restorations did not lower whole-mouth bacteria; ~70% of controls had new cavities within 2 years.
  • Cohort: patients who took the products ≥2× had a ~20% lower DFT increment (1.47 vs 1.82). High-risk regimen: 0.12% CHX daily for 1 week a month + 5000 ppm F toothpaste twice daily.
Paper 1 · Young & Featherstone 2013 · review with example protocols

Caries management by risk assessment

Community Dent Oral Epidemiol 2013;41:e53–e63 (online 2012) · University of the Pacific & UCSF
  • Caries is a disease initiated by a complex biofilm (not one pathogen) that changes with its environment and the local chemistry of tooth, pellicle and saliva — unlike the "one pathogen–one disease" medical model. Management must find which factors are expressing the disease and correct them.
  • CAMBRA = a risk-based approach to prevent, reverse and, when necessary, repair damage using minimally invasive methods. The forms and protocols shown are examples only, and should be kept simple.

The caries balance

Disease indicators — WRECRisk factors — BADProtective factors — SAFER
White spots on smooth surfaces
Restorations in the last 3 years due to caries (last 1 year at recall)
Enamel approximal lesions on radiograph
Cavities / lesions into dentine on radiograph		 Bad (cariogenic) bacteria
Absence of saliva (hyposalivation)
Destructive lifestyle habits (poor diet, frequent fermentable carbohydrate, recreational drugs, poor OH)		 Saliva & sealants
Antibacterials
Fluoride + calcium/phosphate (supports, doesn't replace, fluoride)
Effective lifestyle habits
Risk-based reassessment
  • Disease indicators are physical proof of past or present disease. They don't show the cause or treatment, but are strong predictors. Any one positive → automatically high risk (unless therapy is in place and progress has been arrested). Placing restorations does not significantly lower the overall bacterial challenge.
  • BAD are the three factors proven to be causative. The form lists 9 risk factors: medium/high MS and LB counts · visible heavy plaque · snacking >3× daily between meals · deep pits and fissures · recreational drugs · inadequate saliva flow · saliva-reducing factors (medications, radiation, systemic) · exposed roots · orthodontic appliances.
  • The more severe the risk factors, the more intensive the protective factors must be. The form lists 11 protective factors: fluoridated community · F toothpaste ≥1× and ≥2× daily (twice daily is significantly better) · 0.05% NaF rinse daily · 5000 ppm F toothpaste · F varnish or in-office topical F in the last 6 months · CHX daily for 1 week each month (or another antibacterial) · xylitol 4× daily · Ca/P paste · stimulated saliva >1 mL/min.

Hard-tissue exam, then the risk assessment

  • Previous or current disease is the highest predictor of future disease, so the hard-tissue exam must precede the CRA. Occlusal: ICDAS codes and deep fissures. Approximal: bitewing depth E1, E2, D1, D2, D3 + activity. Facial/lingual (ball-ended probe): active white spots (dull, rough) · inactive white spots (smooth, shiny, hard) · active/inactive brown spots · cavitation in enamel · cavitation into dentine.
  • The CRA draws on medical, dental, social and dietary history. Saliva, pH, buffer and bacterial-load tests have lower levels of evidence, but are useful as teaching and motivating tools.
  • The form: same for every patient; items trimmed to those with a significant relationship to future cavitation (validated by outcomes studies, Doméjean 2006 and 2011); one page; visually weighted by a three-column format (others weight mathematically); patients can fill in parts in the waiting room.
  • Other forms (ADA 0–6 and >6 years; AAPD under 6) differ but all agree caries experience is the strongest predictor; the literature on other factors is very limited, and none of the other forms have published outcomes. 2001 NIH consensus: mutans streptococci alone are no more than weakly predictive.
  • A CRA is mandatory at every initial exam and caries recare visit — risk changes with time.
RiskDefinition
LowVery low risk of future caries, provided no harmful changes are made
ModerateUsed when in doubt between low and high
HighHigh likelihood of new lesions in the next year or two; one or more cavitated lesions
ExtremeHigh risk + major salivary dysfunction (hyposalivation)

Table 1 — SAFER protocol (age 6 to adult)

There is no consensus on the correct protocol. An RCT showed CRA-driven chemical therapy (CHX and/or fluoride) gave a lower caries increment than restorative-only care; multi-intervention care doesn't lend itself well to RCTs and systematic reviews.

RiskSealantsSaliva / bacteriaAntibacterialsFluorideCa/P, pHX-raysRecare
LowNot indicated (optional for deep, at-risk fissures)Optional / baselineNot indicatedOTC F toothpaste bidIf recession or sensitive roots24–36 mo6 mo
ModerateRecommended per ICDAS codeResting and stimulated flow and pH, esp. if hyposalivation suspectedXylitol 2–3×/day, 6–10 g/dayOTC F toothpaste bid + 0.05% NaF rinse bid + varnish every 4–6 moIf low resting pH or low flow18–24 mo4–6 mo

ExtremeAs moderateAs highAs highAs highRequired if xerostomia6 mo until no new lesions3 mo
  • All levels: low-frequency fermentable carbohydrate, adequate protein, effective OH using motivational interviewing; substitute xylitol for sucrose (100% xylitol products; dangerous to dogs).
  • Non-cavitated smooth-surface lesions that don't significantly penetrate the DEJ → treat chemically, not surgically. Extreme risk with multiple cavities → GIC caries control until progression halts, then permanent restorations. Appliances (RPD, ortho) → high-F toothpaste + varnish every 3 months. Use antibacterials alongside fluoride; review at 1 month; a powered brush may help high/extreme risk.

Restorative decisions — site, extent, activity

Bacteria are too large for the diffusion channels of intact enamel, so cavitation through enamel is what should trigger surgical treatment. Caries risk may or may not bear on the restorative decision; sealants are a recommended option for high-risk patients.

Approximal (bitewing)Management
E1 (outer ½ enamel) · E2 (inner ½)Low chance of cavitation → treat chemically (if left untreated, progression to cavitation is likely)
D1 (outer ⅓ dentine)Taught as the "ideal board patient", yet most may not be cavitated → chemical therapy; show progression and/or use elastomeric separation before surgery. Don't justify surgery on high-risk status.
D2 (middle ⅓)Minimally invasive restoration probable but not absolute
D3 (inner ⅓)Minimally invasive restoration needed; conservative removal near the pulp; adequate seal
  • Facial/lingual: visual-tactile assessment makes decisions easy. Active white/brown spots → chemical therapy per CRA; partially cavitated → chemical or MI restoration by clinician–patient discussion; fully cavitated → MI restoration. Root restorations in high-risk patients → a fluoride-releasing material (conventional GIC).
  • Management stages (Table 3): initial — non-surgical (ICDAS 0–2); moderate — minimal removal (ICDAS 3–5); severe — conventional restorative (ICDAS 6).
  • Lesion activity (after Ekstrand): risk status · visual (cavitation/shadow, whitish, brownish) · plaque-stagnation site · rough/soft vs smooth/hard · gingival inflammation/BOP · matt vs shiny · sticky plaque · lesion age <3 or >3 years.
  • Present individualised, evidence-based options with prognosis; help the patient change behaviour with encouragement and clear instructions.
  • Summary: caries is a complex multifactorial disease that cannot be controlled by restoration alone; a CRA predicts risk and identifies which factors are out of balance.
Paper 2 · Featherstone & Chaffee 2018 · summary of UCSF trial and outcome studies

The evidence for caries management by risk assessment (CAMBRA®)

Adv Dent Res 2018;29(1):9–14 · UCSF · 14 years of CAMBRA in the teaching clinics; not a review of others' work
  • Caries = demineralisation by acid from cariogenic bacteria metabolising fermentable carbohydrate; inhibited by salivary components, antibacterials and fluoride; reversed by remineralisation (Ca, PO₄, F).
  • The balance: pathological — (1) cariogenic bacteria, (2) fermentable carbohydrates, (3) salivary dysfunction vs protective — (1) sufficient saliva, (2) remineralisation (Ca, PO₄, F), (3) antibacterials.

The RCT (1999–2005; Featherstone 2012)

UCSF pre-doctoral clinic; adults 18–65 with 1–7 cavities. Control = conventional treatment. Test = fluoride rinse + fluoride toothpaste + 0.12% CHX rinse.

  1. A significant 24% reduction in 2-year caries increment in initially high-risk patients.
  2. Placing restorations had no significant effect on whole-mouth bacterial levels; ~70% of controls returned within 2 years with new cavities.
  3. High baseline decayed surfaces were strongly related to high MS + LB levels.
  4. CHX once daily for 1 week every month markedly reduced cariogenic bacteria (Fig 1). Studies finding no effect used other regimens (e.g. daily for 2 weeks every 3 months).
  5. Re-analysis (Cheng 2015): the reduction was mediated by changes in salivary bacteria and fluoride, plus unmeasured factors.
  6. High-risk patients need antibacterial as well as fluoride therapy.

Development and the 9-step process

Two California consensus conferences; pilots at UCSF and the University of the Pacific from 2003; forms published in 2007.

  1. Dental and medical history
  2. Clinical examination
  3. Detect lesions early enough to reverse or prevent progression
  4. Assess risk — low, moderate, high or extreme (steps 1–3 + a short questionnaire)
  5. Treatment plan including chemical therapy for the risk level
  6. Chemical therapy — fluoride and/or antibacterials by risk
  7. Minimally invasive restorative procedures
  8. Recall at intervals suited to risk
  9. Reassess risk at recall and modify the plan

Validation of the risk assessment

CRA on all new UCSF patients from July 2003; items pared to the strongest predictors. Odds ratios for cavitation or dentine caries at baseline (all significant except fluoridated community in 2006):

Item2006 (n = 2,351)2011 (n = 12,954)
Approximal enamel lesions (radiograph)13.68.2

Fluoride toothpaste0.670.81

Fluoridated community0.81 (NS)0.85
  • Risk was assigned by the individual provider weighing the balance. Extreme = high + hyposalivation (inspection, history, flow rate if in doubt) — about 5% of patients.
  • Example extreme-risk patient: visible cavity, numerous approximal lesions, numerous restorations in 3 years, heavy plaque, frequent snacking, low flow with dry mouth, >1 hyposalivatory medication, once-daily F toothpaste → 7 indicators/pathological factors vs 1 protective.
  • 2011 outcomes (2,571 returning patients): 24% of low-risk had cavities (76% did not — chairside microbiology might improve this negative predictive value); close to 70% of high-risk and 88% of extreme-risk had new cavities. Similar in 2006 and in a new cohort (Chaffee 2015).
  • "Out of the penalty box": new patients are asked about restorations in the past 3 years; patients of record about new caries-related restorations in the past 12 months, so a compliant patient isn't held at high risk for 3 years. Lowering risk motivates patients; Rechmann 2017 showed dramatic falls in risk status within 18–24 months.
  • Ages 0–5 (Ramos-Gomez tool, 2009): very few extreme-risk children, so only low/moderate/high were analysed (n = 3,810 baseline, 1,315 follow-up); ~70% of high-risk children had new decay (Fig 3).

Does treating by risk work? (Chaffee 2015b, retrospective)

18,004 eligible patients (2007–2012); 11,900 adults assessed as high risk; 2,724 examined at follow-up (mean 18 months). Regimen: (1) F varnish at the first visit, (2) 5000 ppm F toothpaste twice daily, (3) 0.12% CHX once daily for 1 week every month, (4) xylitol gum or mints daily. Many declined.

GroupnAdjusted DFT increment
Never took the products1,5011.82
Took them once, never refilled9001.78 (NS vs never)
Took them ≥2 times3231.47 — ~20% lower (significant)
  • Public-assistance subgroup (products free; n = 335 / 238 / 167): ≥2× gave a 38% lower increment — not statistically significant (small numbers).
  • A practice-based trial (18 private practices, 3 community clinics, 460 patients, up to 2 years) showed marked falls in risk status.
  • Evidence base: 2 RCTs + several outcome studies. More RCTs would be ideal (other regimens, lower drop-out, children) but are expensive and hard to fund.

Conclusions

  • The CRA tools "can be used with confidence"; don't modify them without evidence.
  • Adding risk-based chemical therapy reduces caries increment by ~20% in high-risk adults (38% in the insurance-covered subset). Barriers: cost to patients and patient and provider acceptance.
  • High-risk regimen: 0.12% CHX daily for 1 week each month, continued until risk has been reduced for 1 year, + 5000 ppm F toothpaste twice daily. Better antibacterials, microbiome and diet approaches may replace CHX in future.
  • In high-risk people, new cavities keep forming even with water fluoridation and topical fluoride — fluoride must be supplemented by antibacterial therapy.
Compare & contrast
Young & Featherstone 2013Featherstone & Chaffee 2018
PurposeExplain the concept; example forms and protocolsPresent UCSF evidence (RCT + outcome studies)
Balance modelDisease indicators + risk factors vs protective factors (WREC / BAD / SAFER)3 pathological vs 3 protective factors
Antibacterials"Evidence is very limited"; no consensus protocolAntibacterial therapy is necessary with fluoride for high/extreme risk
Common groundBoth co-authored by Featherstone; risk-based chemical therapy plus minimally invasive restoration.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Large cohorts (2,351; 12,954); predictive validity repeated across cohorts.
  • Simple one-page form; preventive, patient-centred, minimally invasive.
  • An RCT supports the chemical regimen; lowering risk motivates patients.
Limitations
  • The developers evaluating their own tool in one university clinic (no conflicts declared) — generalisability to private practice?
  • Odds ratios are associations with caries at baseline; disease indicators are themselves caries.
  • Follow-up only in patients who returned (2,571 of 12,954) and risk assigned by students' judgement.
  • The cohort is retrospective, not randomised — patients who refilled products may differ (adherence); the 38% figure is non-significant.
  • Young admits the antibacterial evidence is "very limited", while F&C call it necessary.
Clinical relevance
  • Hard-tissue exam → CRA at every new-patient and recare visit → set recall and bitewing intervals by risk.
  • Restorations don't control the disease: pair them with risk-matched chemical prevention (5000 ppm F, varnish, NaF rinse, xylitol; CHX for high risk).
  • Manage non-cavitated lesions (E1–D1, ICDAS 1–2, active white spots) chemically and monitor; restore cavitated lesions minimally invasively.
Exam practice
SAQDefine CAMBRA and list its four components.

A concept (not a product or CRA form) for managing caries according to risk: (i) assess the risk of future lesions; (ii) reduce pathological factors; (iii) enhance protective factors; (iv) minimally invasive restorative care.

SAQWhat do WREC, BAD and SAFER stand for?

WREC: White spots, Restorations in the last 3 years, Enamel approximal lesions, Cavities into dentine. BAD: Bad bacteria, Absence of saliva, Destructive lifestyle habits. SAFER: Saliva & sealants, Antibacterials, Fluoride (+Ca/P), Effective lifestyle, Risk-based reassessment.

SAQDefine extreme caries risk and how its management differs from high risk.

High risk (e.g. one or more cavitated lesions) plus hyposalivation. As high risk (5000 ppm F, NaF rinse, varnish every 3–4 months, antibacterials if indicated), but Ca/P/pH supplementation is required if xerostomia, bitewings every 6 months until no new lesions, recare every 3 months; GIC caries control for multiple cavities.

SAQState the main findings of the UCSF RCT.

In high-risk adults, fluoride + 0.12% CHX (once daily for 1 week each month) gave a significant 24% lower 2-year increment. Restorations didn't lower whole-mouth bacteria; ~70% of controls had new cavities within 2 years; the effect was mediated by bacterial and fluoride changes.

SAQHow do Young & Featherstone manage an approximal D1 lesion, and why?

Most D1 lesions may not be cavitated, and intact enamel keeps bacteria out — cavitation is what should trigger surgery. Treat chemically, show progression and/or use elastomeric separation before surgery; high risk alone doesn't justify restoring.

SAQGive three limitations of the CAMBRA evidence.
  • Odds ratios are associations with caries at baseline.
  • Follow-up only in returning patients; the cohort is non-randomised (adherence differences); the 38% reduction is non-significant.
  • Single university clinic; developers assessing their own tool; risk assigned subjectively.
LAQ"Caries cannot be controlled by restoration alone." Discuss with reference to the CAMBRA papers.
  1. Model: caries is a biofilm-driven imbalance between pathological (bacteria, fermentable carbohydrate, salivary dysfunction) and protective factors (saliva, Ca/PO₄/F, antibacterials). Restorations treat the sign, not the balance.
  2. Evidence: RCT — restorations didn't lower whole-mouth bacteria; ~70% of controls had new cavities; CHX + F reduced increment 24%. Cohort — ~20% lower DFT with the regimen. High-risk patients keep developing lesions despite fluoride → antibacterials needed.
  3. Process: hard-tissue exam → CRA (WREC/BAD/SAFER) → risk level → SAFER protocol (fluoride intensity, xylitol, antibacterials, Ca/P, diet, recall and radiograph intervals) → MI restorations only for cavitated/dentine lesions → reassess.
  4. Critique: baseline odds ratios, selection and adherence bias, single centre, developers' own data, Young's "very limited" antibacterial evidence.
  5. Conclusion: risk-based prevention plus MI restoration; the exact chemical regimen is less certain than the principle.
03

ICDAS & ICCMS

  • Detection (is disease present?) · assessment (characterise or monitor a lesion) · diagnosis (the professional summation of all data).
  • ICDAS stages lesions by clinical visual appearance on clean, dry teeth, based on histological extent. Code 1 is seen only when dry; code 2 is visible wet or dry. Codes 3 and 4 were swapped after Baltimore 2005 (ICDAS II; the "II" was later dropped).
  • The ICDAS cube: lesion extent (iceberg) · activity ("is this lesion active today?") · monitoring over time.
  • ICCMS adds patient-level information (including risk) to plan, manage and review caries: 3 principles and 4 elements delivered as a cycle.
  • Iceland: 12-year-olds with "no detectable caries" ranged from 48% to 15% depending on threshold → always state the criteria, e.g. DICDAS 1–6MFT.
Pitts & Ekstrand 2013 · overview by the ICDAS Foundation

International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS) and its International Caries Classification and Management System (ICCMS)

Community Dent Oral Epidemiol 2013;41:e41–e52 · King's College London & University of Copenhagen, on behalf of the ICDAS Foundation
  • ICDAS classifies lesions by their clinical visual appearance. ICCMS integrates ICDAS tooth assessments with patient-level information to plan, manage and review caries.
  • The ICDAS Foundation Coordinating Committee (volunteers since May 2002) aimed for "better quality information to inform decisions about appropriate diagnosis, prognosis and clinical management at both the individual and public health levels".
  • Designed for four domains: clinical practice, education, research and public health.
  • Essential feature: dividing the caries continuum into discrete, predictable categories based on the histological extent of the lesion.

Origins

  • International Consensus Workshop on Caries Clinical Trials (January 2002). A systematic review of earlier classification systems found very variable criteria, many lacking construct validity, making comparison between studies impossible.
  • Consensus separated three terms: lesion detection (objective method of determining whether disease is present), lesion assessment (characterising or monitoring a detected lesion), caries diagnosis (a human professional summation of all available data).
  • The terminology confusion — "a Tower of Babel" — led to an international Glossary, adopted and distributed by the FDI.
  • Existing systems were merged into one (Pitts & Fyffe; Ismail; BASCD; Ekstrand, Ricketts & Kidd; Indiana; Dundee Selectable Threshold Method). Open criteria for clean, dry teeth, avoiding iatrogenic damage from sharp probes.
  • Meetings 2002–2004 (Dundee, Michigan, Indianapolis, Bornholm) → open peer-review workshop at IADR Baltimore 2005 → codes 3 and 4 swapped (ICDAS II). No substantial change since. The underlying ethos is a move from operative to non-operative, preventive care.
  • Workshops in Bogotá (2008), Temple (2010), Montpellier (2010) and Kaunas (2011) developed the ICCMS, which was trademarked by the Foundation (a charity) to keep the open system free and linked to evidence.

The codes and the cube

CodeClinical appearanceMerged stage
0Sound — no caries change after air drying (5 s)Sound
1First visual change in enamel, seen only when dry (or thin change confined to the fissure)A · initial
2Distinct visual change in enamel, visible wet or dry
3Localised enamel breakdown, no visible dentine or shadowB · moderate
4Underlying dark shadow from dentine ± enamel breakdown
5Distinct cavity with visible dentine, involving less than half the surfaceC · extensive
6Extensive distinct cavity with dentine, deep and wide, involving more than half the tooth

Code wording for 0 and 3–6 from Young & Featherstone Table 2 (topic 02); merged stages from Fig 3.

Kaunas 2011 vision statement

ICDAS employs an evidence-based, preventively oriented approach · is a detection and assessment system classifying stages of the caries process · is for education, practice, research and public health · provides a common caries language · has evolved into approved, compatible "formats" · supports decisions at individual and public-health levels · has generated ICCMS to improve long-term outcomes.

The wardrobe

  • Choose the format that suits the task: the full 6-code system (± activity); merged codes — three stages (initial, moderate, extensive); a binary, WHO Basic Methods-like option (obvious dentine caries vs sound). All relate to the "D" of DMF, which can still be calculated at tooth or surface level; PUFA can also be used.
  • Not everyone needs all 6 codes, but full codes let clinicians judge the success of prevention on non-cavitated lesions. The FDI Caries Matrix is also compatible.
  • Training: a free 90-minute e-learning programme (English, Spanish, German, Portuguese) and a 52-slide PowerPoint pack. By May 2012: 88 peer-reviewed publications, 6 books/chapters and 45 other publications, with first authors from 19 countries. The Alliance for a Cavity-Free Future ("Stop Caries NOW") uses ICDAS.

ICCMS

3 guiding principles
  1. Prevention (primary and secondary) as a priority; surgery only as a last resort.
  2. Where surgery is indicated, minimal removal of tooth tissue.
  3. Cavity size and material selection governed by preservation of tooth tissue and healthy outcomes.

Covers the full spectrum: health → initial, moderate, extensive lesions → pain and sepsis.

4 key elements (a cycle)
  1. Initial patient assessments — histories and data collection.
  2. Lesion detection, activity and appropriate risk assessment — e.g. Cariogram or CAMBRA.
  3. Synthesis and decision-making — patient-level + lesion-level information.
  4. Clinical treatments (non-surgical and surgical) with prevention.

Revisited cyclically with monitoring and review at risk-based intervals, via Caries Management Pathways.

  • Links to the FDI Global Caries Initiative and an "upstream" common risk factor approach, helping reduce health inequalities. In primary care, prevention and long-term maintenance are the priorities; reimbursement systems need upgrading to reward this.
  • The ICDAS framework has been used extensively in Japan — working well for patients and dentists and financially viable.

The four domains

  • Clinical practice: visual examination of clean, dry teeth is the foundation, plus lesion detection aids (radiographs, adjuncts). Electrical methods and laser fluorescence may be useful adjuncts, especially occlusally — but evidence is limited. Activity assessment is very important for deciding when preventive options are appropriate. Feasibility tested in UK general practice and Europe; part of the Scottish SDCEP Oral Health Assessment guidance (used from Denmark to New Zealand).
  • Education: ICCMS specified by 11 international dental schools; ORCA/ADEE European Core Curriculum in Cariology (5 key areas). Planning for initial (1–2) and extensive (5–6) caries is often straightforward; moderate caries (3–4) needs real clinical decision-making skill.
  • Research: compatible staging in research and practice shortens translation time. IADR GOHIRA (inequalities agenda); a programme training examiners in 8 Latin American countries for children under 6.
  • Public health: full or merged codes; backward-compatible D₃MFT/S can be computed. Approved field modification: gauze drying with codes 1 and 2 merged into "A" (the EADPH found portable air feasible). Dual coding records restoration/sealant status as well as caries.
Iceland survey — "no detectable caries", permanent teethAge 12Age 15
D3 threshold, clinical visual48%35%
D1 threshold, clinical visual34%20%
D3 threshold, visual + radiographic22%16%
D1 threshold, visual + radiographic15%6%

D1 = enamel and dentine caries; D3 = dentine caries only. Kaunas recommendation: report with a subscript listing the codes counted, e.g. DICDAS 1–6MFT (D1) or DICDAS 4–6MFT (D3) — regions use different D3 cut-offs.

Next steps: iPad epidemiology software (choose decay threshold, tooth or surface, age and sex), web and e-learning updates, and a book (Clinical Management of Dental Caries). Conclusion: ICDAS gives flexible, increasingly adopted methods for staging caries and activity; ICCMS integrates tooth and patient information, including risk, to plan, manage and review caries.

Contrasting viewpoint — ICDAS/ICCMS vs CAMBRA
ICDAS / ICCMSCAMBRA
FocusLesion staging and activity, inside a management cyclePatient risk and chemical therapy
LinkICCMS names CAMBRA or Cariogram for its risk step; Young & Featherstone use ICDAS codes for occlusal decisions. Both are preventive and minimally invasive.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • International consensus; open and free; a common language.
  • Stages linked to histological extent, plus activity and monitoring.
  • Flexible formats that stay compatible with DMF and PUFA.
Limitations
  • Written by the system's own developers; promotional in tone; industry educational grants acknowledged (Colgate, Smile-on, J&J, Cadbury, CariesScan).
  • An overview — no original data or accuracy statistics.
  • Full coding needs training, clean dry teeth and air; detection adjuncts have limited evidence; uptake depends on reimbursement.
Clinical relevance
  • Clean, dry teeth, good light, ball-ended probe — no sharp explorer.
  • Record stage and activity, and monitor over time. Initial lesions → prevention; extensive → operative; moderate (3–4) need careful judgement.
  • State the threshold whenever caries data are compared.
Exam practice
SAQDistinguish lesion detection, lesion assessment and caries diagnosis.

Detection = an objective method of determining whether disease is present. Assessment = characterising or monitoring a lesion once detected. Diagnosis = a human professional summation of all available data.

SAQDescribe ICDAS codes 1–6.

1: first visual change in enamel, seen only when dry. 2: distinct visual change, visible wet or dry. 3: localised enamel breakdown, no visible dentine or shadow. 4: underlying dark shadow from dentine. 5: distinct cavity with visible dentine, less than half the surface. 6: extensive distinct cavity, more than half the tooth. (0 = sound.)

SAQExplain the three faces of the ICDAS cube.

Front: detecting lesion extent (the iceberg, linked to background care, preventive and operative options). Top: assessing activity — "is this lesion active today?". Side: monitoring lesion behaviour over time (e.g. code 2 → 3 → 4 vs 2 → 0).

SAQList the three ICCMS principles and four key elements.

Principles: prevention first, surgery as a last resort; minimal tissue removal; cavity size and material governed by tissue preservation. Elements: initial patient assessments; lesion detection, activity and risk assessment; synthesis and decision-making; clinical treatment with prevention — as a cycle with risk-based review.

SAQWhat does the Iceland survey show, and what did the Kaunas workshop recommend?

"No detectable caries" in 12-year-olds ranged from 48% (D3, visual) to 15% (D1, visual + radiographs) — prevalence depends on threshold and method. Report the codes counted, e.g. DICDAS 1–6MFT or DICDAS 4–6MFT.

LAQCritically discuss ICDAS/ICCMS as a framework for caries management, comparing it with CAMBRA.
  1. Background: inconsistent earlier criteria lacking construct validity → consensus, glossary, merged systems; detection vs assessment vs diagnosis.
  2. ICDAS: codes 0–6 on clean dry teeth by histological extent; activity; cube; wardrobe (full, merged, basic, DMF, PUFA); the 3/4 swap.
  3. ICCMS: 3 principles, 4-element cycle including risk (CAMBRA/Cariogram), risk-based review, upstream approach, reimbursement.
  4. Comparison: lesion-level (ICDAS) vs patient-level (CAMBRA) — complementary.
  5. Appraisal: common language and preventive ethos vs developer authorship, no original data, training burden, limited evidence for adjuncts; moderate lesions (3–4) need judgement.
04

Managing carious lesions — the ICCC consensus

  • Dental caries is the disease (a biofilm ecological shift driven by fermentable carbohydrate); the carious lesion is its sign. Caries can't be removed — only carious tissue. Caries management = patient level, non-invasive; carious lesion management = tooth level, on a non-cleansable lesion.
  • Dentine is described by feel: soft → leathery → firm → hard. Approaches: no removal · selective removal (to soft or to firm) · stepwise removal · non-selective removal to hard (overtreatment, not advocated).
  • Shallow/moderate lesions → selective removal to firm (restoration longevity first). Deep lesions → selective removal to soft (pulpal health first), or stepwise in permanent teeth only.
  • Restore only when a cavitated lesion is non-cleansable and can no longer be sealed. The only evidence-based reason left for removing carious tissue is a large enough surface to bond to.
  • Hardness is the primary criterion · no evidence for cavity disinfection · liners aren't needed to control a sealed lesion · repair rather than replace.
Paper 1 · Innes 2016 · consensus on terminology

Managing carious lesions: consensus recommendations on terminology

Adv Dent Res 2016;28(2):49–57 · International Caries Consensus Collaboration (ICCC): 21 cariology experts from 12 countries, Leuven, February 2015

Why new terms were needed

  • The same procedure had different names (Franzon's "one-step excavation" ≈ Hesse's "partial caries removal"), and the same name meant different procedures (Maltz and Hesse both said "partial" removal but described different end points). Mertz-Fairhurst 1998 is quoted as a model of clear description.
  • Method: 7 systematic reviews of caries-removal methods yielded 23 terms; members added 19 → 42 terms for essentially 4 parts of the spectrum. Each member chose up to 6 representative terms → 8 naming approaches → discussed at the meeting.
  • History: 150 years ago, removing all carious tissue plus Black's "extension for prevention" was the gold standard. The paradigm then shifted to removing only infected, not affected, dentine (Fusayama). Options now range from complete surgical excision to no removal with non-invasive control.

Agreed basics

  • Caries ≠ carious lesion. Dental caries (the process) can't be removed — only carious tissue. A lesion can be stabilised by non-invasive or invasive means.
  • Caries management = patient-level control of the disease by preventive, non-invasive means (plaque control, fluoride, diet, behaviour change). Carious lesion management = doing something to an established, non-cleansable lesion to stop it progressing — removing none, some or all carious tissue. Patient-level management is still needed ("the cause of the cause").
  • Say "removal", not "excavation" (excavation implies hand excavators).
  • Primary aim of carious tissue removal: retain the tooth, and the health (sensibility/vitality) of its pulp, for as long as possible.
  • Guiding principles: preserve dental tissue · maintain pulpal health · avoid pulp exposure · avoid dental anxiety · sound cavity margins for a peripheral seal.
  • "Complete" removal was ambiguous: the group meant to leathery or firm dentine pulpally, but many believe it means to hard dentine. Removal to hard dentine throughout is overtreatment. "Firm" and "hard" are subjective but were the best terms available.

Histology vs clinical feel

  • Clinical appearance can't be related directly to histopathology. Example of a misreading: early lateral spread at the EDJ was thought to undermine sound enamel, which led to early operative intervention and tunnel preparations. Lateral spread is actually a sequel of the clinically exposed dentine lesion (retrograde demineralisation of enamel from the EDJ).
  • Histological terms are less useful chairside, and "infected" is outdated — it implies caries is a communicable disease.
DentineDefinition
SoftDeforms when a hard instrument is pressed onto it; easily scooped up (e.g. sharp hand excavator) with little force.
LeatheryDoes not deform under an instrument but can still be lifted easily without much force. A transition between soft and firm; there may be little difference from firm.
FirmPhysically resistant to hand excavation; some pressure is needed to lift it.
HardA pushing force is needed to engage it, and only a sharp cutting edge or a bur will lift it. A straight probe gives a scratchy sound — the "cri dentinaire".

The approaches (Table 1)

ApproachWhat is doneIndications (non-cleansable dentine lesions)
ARTHand instruments only. Remove soft, completely demineralised tissue until firm resistance is felt (leave some soft dentine pulpally in deep lesions). Restore and seal pits and fissures with an adhesive material, usually high-viscosity GIC.Primary & permanent: shallow and moderate lesions
No removal: sealantResin or GIC sealant (including therapeutic "ART sealants") over intact enamel or early breakdown. "Trampoline effect" concern (soft dentine under weakened enamel) → limit to lesions in the outer ⅓ of dentine on radiographs, pending evidence.Primary & permanent: shallow/moderate lesions that look non-cavitated but may reach dentine radiographically
No removal: Hall techniquePreformed stainless steel crown cemented with GIC over a primary molar — no preparation, no caries removal. Seals the lesion, slows or stops progression; the tooth exfoliates without pain or infection.Primary: moderate/deep proximal lesions (cavitated or not) with a clear band of dentine before the pulp. Permanent: not indicated.
No removal: non-restorative cavity controlOpen the cavity so the patient or parent can clean it with a toothbrush; intensive prevention (fluoride toothpaste ± varnish ± GI-based material). Also called non-restorative caries treatment or slicing.Primary & permanent: cavitated lesions that can be made cleansable (mostly primary; permanent e.g. root caries)
Selective removal to softSoft dentine left pulpally; periphery hard. Remove enough for a durable restoration without exposure. Formerly partial, one-step, ultraconservative or incomplete removal.Primary & permanent: deep lesions
Selective removal to firmLeathery/firm dentine left pulpally; periphery hard. Removes contaminated but not demineralised (remineralisable) dentine.Primary & permanent: shallow/moderate lesions
Stepwise removalStage 1: selective removal to soft + a provisional restoration that can last up to 12 months. Stage 2 (6–12 months later): selective removal to firm + definitive restoration.Permanent: deep lesions. Primary: not indicated (use selective to soft)
Non-selective removal to hardHard dentine everywhere, including pulpally (formerly "complete caries removal").Not advocated — overtreatment; in deep lesions risks exposure, pulp irritation through thin dentine and needless weakening of the tooth

Shallow/moderate = outer ⅔ or ¾ of dentine radiographically, or no risk of exposure. Deep = inner (pulpal) ⅓ or ¼ of dentine radiographically, or a clinically assessed risk of exposure.

Why "selective"?

  • "Complete" and "incomplete" describe the result, but the end point (free of bacteria? demineralised? discoloured? soft?) was never agreed, can't be measured chairside, and re-testing would find residual tissue after "complete" removal and vice versa → use a procedural definition of what was done.
  • A new term with no baggage; "partial" and "incomplete" implied sub-optimal treatment.
  • Selective removal uses different criteria at the periphery (sound enamel and hard, scratchy dentine for the best adhesive seal) and pulpally. "Stepwise" was kept because it was already used consistently.
  • Still to standardise: "invasive", "restorative", "intervention". Dissemination planned through ORCA, the IADR Cariology Group and the ADEA Cariology Section.
Paper 2 · Schwendicke 2016 · consensus recommendations

Managing carious lesions: consensus recommendations on carious tissue removal

Adv Dent Res 2016;28(2):58–67 · ICCC · graded for/against and strong/weak after appraising evidence and discussion · retainable teeth with sensible pulps or reversible pulpitis

When to intervene restoratively

  • Caries is not an infectious disease to be "cured" by removing bacteria; it is managed behaviourally by controlling carbohydrate supply and biofilm. Left uncontrolled, the lesion progresses → chronic pulp inflammation → necrosis and apical periodontitis.
  • Aims for existing lesions: inactivate the disease · preserve hard tissue · avoid starting the re-restoration cycle · keep the tooth as long as possible. Key question: "When do I need to intervene restoratively (invasively)?"
  • Non-cavitated (cleansable) lesions → biofilm removal, remineralisation, or sealing (fissure sealant occlusally; sealing or resin infiltration proximally). Cavitated lesions the patient can clean can be inactivated without restoration; non-cleansable ones may be made cleansable by widening the opening (mostly primary teeth).
  • Once the surface is cavitated, a lesion is non-cleansable and active until proven otherwise. Proximally, separation, radiographs and FOTI help but aren't definitive — also weigh caries risk and radiographic depth. "Microcavitation" is not an agreed term.
  • Non-cleansable cavitated dentine lesions can't be controlled by biofilm removal, remineralisation or sealing alone. Occlusal lesions that look intact but reach well into dentine on radiographs can be sealed if biofilm control fails — monitor the sealant (trampoline effect → failure → restore).
Why restore? (Kidd 2004)
  1. Aid plaque control and so manage activity at that site
  2. Protect the pulp–dentine complex and arrest the lesion by sealing it
  3. Restore function, form and aesthetics
Old reasons for removal — rebutted
  • Retain the restoration — applies only to amalgam.
  • Remove bacteria — a tight seal reduces their viability and cariogenicity; no clinical harm to the pulp from sealing bacteria in (Ricketts 2013).
  • Remove demineralised dentine — structurally intact demineralised dentine can remineralise.
  • Left: create a surface to bond to, and remove enough soft dentine for a restoration of sufficient bulk.
  • Trade-off: in deep lesions, prioritise pulpal health; in shallow/moderate lesions, restoration longevity. Pulp sensibility tests are of doubtful validity, but against the risks of necrosis, infection and a potentially poorer prognosis than root canal treatment of a vital pulp, preserving pulpal health is favoured.
  • Principles during removal: preserve non-demineralised and remineralisable tissue · seal on sound enamel/dentine at the periphery · avoid pain and anxiety · maintain pulpal health by preserving residual dentine (can't be measured clinically) and avoiding exposure.

Choosing the strategy

  • Selective to firm — leathery dentine left pulpally, periphery hard (scratchy). Treatment of choice in both dentitions for shallow/moderate lesions; in deeper lesions it carries significant pulpal risk.
  • Selective to soft — soft dentine over the pulp avoids exposure and pulpal "stress"; significantly lowers the exposure risk compared with removal to hard or firm.
  • Stepwise — the provisional must last up to 12 months, partly because patients may not return. Rationale: tertiary dentine forms, demineralised dentine remineralises, viable bacteria fall. On re-entry, reassess colour and hardness (drier = less active) and remove only until leathery dentine remains over the pulp. Some evidence that the second step can be omitted — it raises exposure risk and adds cost, time and discomfort. Not needed in primary teeth (limited life span).
  • Assessing removal: hardness, moisture, colour, fluorescence, dye uptake; self-limiting burs and chemomechanical methods. Most are validated only in vitro; caries-detector dyes are even detrimental. All are surrogates to be validated against pain, pulpal health and tooth retention. Harder, darker, drier dentine = arrest.
  • Methods (hand, burs, air- or sono-abrasion, chemomechanical, lasers): evidence is sparse; hand or chemomechanical removal may reduce pain and discomfort.
  • Cavity disinfection: theoretically flawed (bacterial numbers matter little under a tight seal; effects are superficial) and adds time and cost.
  • Liners (traditionally Ca(OH)₂): not needed to control a sealed lesion — remineralisation is pulp-mediated. Thermal insulation matters under amalgam. Under composite, a liner may block monomer penetration and protect low-modulus carious dentine from fracturing under shrinkage stress. Calcium silicates may prove beneficial.

Restorative materials

MaterialForAgainst
AmalgamGood longevity, especially in high caries risk (corrosion products seal the margin; antibacterial)Unaesthetic; being phased down (Minamata Treaty, Oct 2013)
Resin compositeLongevity now similar to amalgamMore secondary caries in high-risk patients. Bond strength to carious dentine is lower than to sound dentine and ∝ bonded area → leave carious dentine only over the pulp; the periphery must support and seal
GIC (high-viscosity)Biocompatible, releases fluoride, bonds chemically. HV-GIC (ART) survival no different from amalgam, or from composite in children → primary teeth and single-surface permanent cavitiesLess aesthetic, more early wear; mechanical failure in large, loaded proximal cavities (older trials)
Indirect (inlay, onlay, crown)—More invasive and more expensive

A radiolucency under a restoration with an intact seal and no pulpal symptoms → monitor, don't replace. Reseal, refurbish, repolish or repair whenever possible.

The 14 recommendations

#RecommendationStrength
1Manage the disease and control lesion activity to preserve tissue, avoid starting the restorative cycle and retain the toothStrong
2Restore when a cavitated lesion is non-cleansable and sealing is no longer an optionStrong
3Restorations aid biofilm control, protect the pulp–dentine complex and restore function, form and aesthetics; not all contaminated or demineralised tissue near the pulp needs removingStrong
4Deep lesions → prioritise pulpal health; shallow/moderate → restoration longevityStrong
5Shallow/moderate lesions → selective removal to firmWeak
6Deep lesions (primary and permanent) → selective removal to softStrong
7Deep lesions in permanent teeth → stepwise is also an optionStrong
8Hardness is the primary criterion for assessing and reporting removalWeak
9Moisture, colour, optical properties and bacterial metabolites may be additional indicatorsWeak
10No single removal method recommended; hand or chemomechanical removal may reduce pain and anxiety, especially in childrenWeak
11No evidence of patient benefit from cavity disinfectionWeak
12Liners aren't needed to control a sealed lesion but may help against monomer penetration and dentine fracture under compositeWeak
13Choose the material by lesion location and extent, caries risk, activity, patient and setting; no material is proven best after selective removalWeak
14Repair (reseal, refurbish, repolish) where possible; replacement is the last resortStrong

Knowledge gaps (15–20, all strong): report lesion depth, activity and extent, patient risk and age, setting, operator and technique in the agreed terms · use outcomes that matter to stakeholders (validate surrogates) · long-term follow-up and harms · test removal strategies combined with liners, adhesives and materials · basic research on pulpal reactions · an accurate clinical test of pulpal health.

Compare & contrast
Innes 2016Schwendicke 2016
QuestionWhat do we call it?What should we do?
MethodTerms from 7 systematic reviews + members (42) → consensusAppraised evidence + discussion → graded recommendations
OutputDisease vs lesion; soft/leathery/firm/hard; approaches with indications (Table 1)14 recommendations (7 strong, 7 weak), decision tree, 6 knowledge gaps
Shared viewSame group and meeting (Edwina Kidd presented). Schwendicke takes the aims of restoration from Kidd 2004 (topic 05).
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • International group (21 experts, 12 countries) drawing on systematic reviews and trials.
  • Procedural, unambiguous definitions; graded recommendations plus a research agenda.
  • Full declaration of interests; sponsors had no role and weren't present; no honoraria.
  • Patient-centred: protects the pulp, limits anxiety and the restorative cycle.
Limitations
  • Expert consensus; no formal grading or voting method is described.
  • Industry-sponsored meeting (GC, DMG, 3M ESPE, Dentsply paid travel); several authors had industry links; one expert (Buchalla) declined authorship because he didn't support the content.
  • Half the recommendations are weak — including selective removal to firm.
  • Tactile terms are subjective (leathery ≈ firm); contaminated vs demineralised dentine can't be told apart chairside; pulp tests are of doubtful validity.
  • End-point criteria mostly validated in vitro; stepwise relies on the patient returning; the sealant "trampoline effect" is unresolved.
Clinical relevance
  • First ask whether the lesion is cleansable or sealable; restore only if it isn't.
  • Periphery to sound enamel and hard dentine for the seal. Pulpally: firm for shallow/moderate, soft for deep; stepwise is an option in deep permanent lesions; Hall or selective to soft in deep primary molars.
  • Judge by hardness; skip caries-detector dyes and cavity disinfection; use a liner only for a reason.
  • Monitor a radiolucency under a sound, symptom-free restoration; repair before replacing.
Exam practice
SAQDefine soft, leathery, firm and hard dentine.

Soft: deforms under a hard instrument; scooped up easily with little force. Leathery: doesn't deform but can still be lifted easily. Firm: resists hand excavation; some pressure needed to lift it. Hard: needs a pushing force to engage; only a sharp cutting edge or bur lifts it; a probe gives a scratchy "cri dentinaire".

SAQDifferentiate caries management from carious lesion management.

Caries management = patient-level control of the disease by preventive, non-invasive means (plaque control, fluoride, diet, behaviour change). Carious lesion management = tooth-level action on an established, non-cleansable lesion to stop it progressing (removing none, some or all carious tissue). Patient-level management is still needed alongside it.

SAQGive the three traditional reasons for removing carious tissue and the ICCC's response to each.
  • Retention — only relevant to amalgam, not adhesive materials.
  • Remove bacteria — a tight seal reduces their viability and cariogenicity; sealing bacteria in hasn't harmed the pulp clinically.
  • Remove demineralised dentine — structurally intact demineralised dentine can remineralise.

The only evidence-based reason left is a large enough surface to bond to (plus enough room for a durable restoration).

SAQWhich removal strategy is recommended for (a) a moderate lesion and (b) a deep lesion in a permanent molar with a vital, asymptomatic pulp?

(a) Selective removal to firm, periphery to hard — restoration longevity (weak recommendation). (b) Selective removal to soft (strong) or stepwise removal (strong): stage 1 to soft + provisional, re-enter at 6–12 months to firm — pulpal health first. ART is also listed in the decision tree.

SAQDescribe the Hall technique and its indications.

A preformed stainless steel crown cemented with GIC over a primary molar with no preparation and no caries removal. It seals the lesion, slowing or stopping progression, so the tooth exfoliates without pain or infection. Indicated for moderate/deep proximal lesions (cavitated or not) with a radiographic band of dentine between lesion and pulp. Not indicated in permanent teeth.

SAQWhy is stepwise removal not used in primary teeth, and why might the second step be omitted in permanent teeth?

Primary teeth have a limited life span, so selective removal to soft is done instead. In permanent teeth, re-entry raises the risk of pulp exposure and adds cost, time and discomfort; there is some evidence the second step can be skipped. Patients may also not return.

LAQUsing the 2016 ICCC papers, explain how and why contemporary carious tissue removal differs from traditional "complete caries removal".
  1. Disease concept: caries is a biofilm-driven ecological shift managed behaviourally — you can't remove caries, only carious tissue; caries management (patient) vs carious lesion management (tooth).
  2. Traditional approach: removal of all carious tissue + extension for prevention; "complete" was ambiguous and removal to hard dentine throughout is overtreatment (exposure, pulp irritation, weakened tooth, restorative cycle).
  3. Why change: retention matters only for amalgam; a tight seal inactivates bacteria; demineralised dentine remineralises → the only remaining reason is a bondable surface and room for a durable restoration.
  4. Terms and approaches: soft/leathery/firm/hard; no removal (sealant, Hall, NRCC), selective (to firm, to soft), stepwise, non-selective (not advocated); ART.
  5. Decision: cleansable/sealable → non-restorative. Otherwise by depth and dentition (shallow/moderate → firm; deep → soft, or stepwise in permanent teeth; Hall in primary molars). Periphery hard; hardness as the criterion; no disinfection; liners optional; repair rather than replace.
  6. Critique: expert consensus, half the recommendations weak, subjective tactile terms, unreliable pulp tests, in-vitro surrogates, industry sponsorship.
05

How clean must a cavity be? Minimally invasive caries removal

  • Kidd: the biofilm drives caries; a restoration's job is to restore a surface the patient can clean and to seal — so "how clean?" may be irrelevant. There is no clear evidence that leaving infected dentine, even soft and wet, under a seal is harmful.
  • Tomes 1859: leave discoloured dentine to protect the pulp. Black 1908: better to expose the pulp than leave it covered with softened dentine.
  • Evidence: sealed lesions arrest; stepwise excavation gives fewer exposures (15 vs 53%; 17.5 vs 40%); re-entry dentine is drier, harder, darker with fewer, less cariogenic bacteria; Mertz-Fairhurst lesions sealed over soft dentine stayed arrested for 10 years. Caries-detector dye leads to over-preparation.
  • Banerjee (the ICCC recommendations rewritten for practitioners): "any lesion at any stage of its progression can arrest". After preventive control, selective removal should be the norm, guided by hardness (soft = "sticky", leathery = "tacky").
  • Low-anxiety methods: ART, Hall technique, chemomechanical gel (Carisolv). The second stage of stepwise removal may be omitted; cavity disinfection has no evidence base.
Paper 1 · Kidd 2004 · narrative review

How 'clean' must a cavity be before restoration?

Caries Res 2004;38:305–313 · Guy's, King's and St Thomas' Dental Institute, London · not systematic — the studies' methods were too disparate

The argument

  • Caries is a dynamic process in the biofilm; the lesion reflects biofilm activity and can be modified by disturbing the plaque (brushing with fluoride toothpaste; fluoride controls the rate of progression).
  • A cavity retains biofilm that brushing can't reach, so operative dentistry restores the surface so the patient can clean. Once cavitated, the dentine is infected: is caries driven by the surface biofilm, the infected dentine, or both? If only the biofilm, what matters is sealing the hole. Yet removing infected tissue and filling teeth "has spawned a profession, a public and political paymasters" who consider it essential.
"It is better that a layer of discoloured dentine should be allowed to remain for the protection of the pulp rather than run the risk of sacrificing the tooth." — John Tomes, 1859
"It is better to expose the pulp of a tooth than to leave it covered only with softened dentine." — G.V. Black, 1908

Pulpo-dentinal reactions

  • When acid production stops (biofilm disturbed), the lesion arrests and the demineralised tissue remains as a scar. Non-cavitated enamel lesions have little or no bacterial invasion.
  • Once a cavity forms, biofilm in the hole infects the dentine, which spreads laterally along the EDJ at the cavity edges. One lesion can progress slowly where it is open and cleaned and rapidly where plaque is sheltered by undermined enamel. Massler 1967: distinguish active from arrested lesions.
  • Slow lesions: peritubular mineralisation narrows the tubules (sclerosis) and reactionary tertiary dentine forms (more irregular the more active the lesion) → protects the pulp.
  • Rapid lesions: odontoblasts destroyed, no tertiary dentine; microbial products pass through permeable dentine → reversible or irreversible pulpitis ± pain. If the cariogenic environment changes, new odontoblast-like cells may form reparative dentine.
  • Root caries: dentine is infected early, yet active lesions became inactive within months with cleaning and fluoride — no need to cut infected dentine away. But under a coronal restoration the patient can't brush: what happens to the organisms "entombed" by the dentist?

Evidence 1 — sealants over carious dentine (Table 1)

StudyFollow-upFinding
Jeronimus 1975Up to 4 weeksMany sealants lost; under intact ones dentine dry, dark, leathery; bacteria fell in shallow lesions, persisted in deeper ones
Handelman 19760–2 yearsNo increase in radiographic depth; large fall in bacteria vs untreated controls
Going 19785 yearsArrested; sterile or far fewer bacteria on re-entry, but S. mutans and lactobacilli survived
Mertz-Fairhurst 19796–12 monthsSealed lesions didn't deepen (controls did); no micro-organisms; sealed dentine powdery, dry, white over hard glassy dentine; controls spongy, soft, yellow
Jensen & Handelman 19800–12 monthsEtching alone cut bacteria by 75%; counts fell with time under sealant
Handelman 19812–5 yearsLesion depth decreased while the sealant stayed intact
Mertz-Fairhurst 19861–17 monthsUnsealed lesions deepened, sealed ones didn't; all but one sealed lesion free of micro-organisms
Weerheijm 1992 (outlier)RetrospectiveRadiolucency under clinically intact sealants; cariogenic bacteria in 50%; dentine soft, moist, dark — but no pre-sealing sample to compare

Themes: sealed lesions arrested clinically and radiographically; bacteria fell or disappeared; no pulpitis; lesions progressed only where sealants were lost or absent.

Classical excavation and its problems

  • It assumes both biofilm and dentine bacteria drive caries — yet some bacteria remain even when all soft dentine is removed (Lager 2003).
  • EDJ: some schools teach stain-free as well as hard, but bacteria remain whatever is done → logical to leave stain there. Pulpally: leave "firm and leathery" dentine where removal might expose the pulp, under a Ca(OH)₂ liner (which reduces bacteria) = indirect pulp capping. But one teacher's "firm and leathery" is another's "rather soft".
  • Caries-detector dye (Fusayama: acid red in propylene glycol) was meant to separate irreversibly damaged infected dentine from remineralisable affected dentine. It does not discriminate them → over-preparation at the EDJ and over the pulp.
  • Dry, crumbly dentine under old restorations is minimally infected — probably caries a previous dentist left behind. Soft, wet dentine may likewise be arrestable simply by sealing it in.

Evidence 2 — stepwise excavation (Table 2)

Described by Bodecker: remove only part of the soft dentine at the first visit (acute phase) → restore → re-open weeks later → excavate further → definitive restoration. Aim: arrest the lesion and let tertiary dentine form so exposure is less likely. Most studies were uncontrolled, in deep lesions in permanent teeth, with varied first-stage removal, materials and re-entry times (3 weeks to 2 years).

StudyFinding
Law & Lewis 196176% clinically and radiographically successful
King 1965Sterile on re-entry: Ca(OH)₂ 61.4%, ZOE 81.8%, amalgam 0% (though fewer organisms)
Kerkhove 196792% success; dentine dry, hard, brownish-yellow and more radio-opaque
Kreulen 1997 · Weerheijm 1999Large fall in viable counts, mutans streptococci and lactobacilli — more under RMGIC than amalgam (Kreulen: dentine darker and harder)
Bjørndal & Thylstrup 19985 of 94 exposed at final excavation; 88 symptom-free at 1 year
Bjørndal & Larsen 2000Fewer lactobacilli and gram-negative rods; flora dominated by Actinomyces naeslundii and streptococci
Maltz 2002Dentine drier, harder, darker; more radio-opaque; counts fell significantly

Themes: (1) high success — exposure usually avoided, symptoms rare between visits (controls often exposed); (2) dentine drier, harder, darker on re-entry; (3) far smaller cultivable flora, some teeth sterile, shifted to a less cariogenic flora; (4) a possible effect of the material, rarely tested properly.

Why re-enter? To confirm there is no exposure and remove the remaining infected dentine. But the depth of the first excavation didn't affect how infected the dentine was at re-entry, and if the biofilm drives caries, sealing alone should arrest it — the surviving bacteria may be "opportunistic squatters". Indirect pulp capping already doesn't re-enter.

Evidence 3 — RCTs of "complete" vs "incomplete" removal (Table 3)

TrialDesignResult
Magnusson & Sundell 1977Deep lesions, primary teeth: stepwise (re-entry 4–6 weeks) vs complete removalExposed 15% vs 53%; 2 cases of pulpitis between visits
Leskell 1996Deep lesions, permanent teeth: stepwise (8–24 weeks) vs complete removalExposed 17.5% vs 40%
Mertz-Fairhurst 1998Occlusal lesions ≤ halfway into dentine. Soft, moist, infected dentine left at the EDJ and over the pulp under a bonded, sealed composite (n = 156) vs amalgam + sealant (77) vs conventional amalgam (79). No re-entry10 years: lesions arrested (one "caved in"); no more failures than controls; some conventional amalgams failed with new marginal caries
Ribeiro 1999Primary teeth: EDJ caries-free, soft dentine left over the pulp + composite (24) vs dye-guided complete removal (24); 1 yearAll retained; radiographically 46% regressed, 25% progressed, 29% unchanged; 1 pulp necrosis among controls

The deep-lesion trials strongly support a stepwise approach to avoid exposure; the trials in shallower lesions show that sealing incompletely excavated cavities didn't harm restoration performance.

Conclusion — "uncomfortable reading for those of us teaching operative dentistry"

No clear evidence that leaving infected dentine — even soft and wet — before sealing is harmful. The cautious approach may be preferable: fewer exposures; sealing encourages arrest, tubular sclerosis and tertiary dentine (less permeable dentine). The residual bacteria are entombed between the restoration's seal and the less permeable dentine — biologically logical if the biofilm drives caries.

Further research: the fate of residual bacteria (survival, phenotypic or genotypic change, slow demineralisation, pulpal reaction). Bacterial-leakage studies (Bergenholtz 1982) used caries-free teeth, where preparation opens millions of tubules. Needed: in-vivo pulp monitoring; RCTs of stepwise in shallow vs deep lesions, depth of removal, medicament, material and re-entry time; bacteria-killing methods (ozone, photo-activated disinfection); and stable populations for long-term trials like Mertz-Fairhurst's.

Paper 2 · Banerjee 2017 · consensus recommendations for practitioners

Contemporary operative caries management: consensus recommendations on minimally invasive caries removal

Br Dent J 2017;223(3):215–222 · BDJ Minimum Intervention themed issue · modified from Schwendicke 2016 (topic 04) on behalf of the ICCC · cavitated lesions with vital or reversibly inflamed pulps

Context

  • Caries prevalence has fallen over three decades, but caries is still the most prevalent disease worldwide. Research–practice gap: inconsistent guidelines, dental education relying on outdated concepts, national health policies and remuneration systems.
  • Traditional "drill and fill" removed all carious tissue in the erroneous belief that this stops caries. Caries is not an infection to be cured by removing bacteria; it is managed behaviourally. Left unchecked it leads to pulpal inflammation, pain and infection.
  • If the biofilm is regularly disturbed, "any lesion at any stage of its progression can arrest" (Fig 1). Restoration is needed when patient behaviour prevents this, or to restore lost structure, form or aesthetics.
Why restore — then vs now

Historical: (1) withstand packing and retain the restoration (amalgam); (2) remove bacteria to stop caries; (3) remove demineralised, discoloured dentine.

Now: adhesive, bioactive materials make large-scale removal unjustified. A good peripheral seal reduces the viability and cariogenicity of remaining bacteria, so removing tissue (or disinfecting) to kill bacteria isn't logical. Demineralised but structurally intact dentine can remineralise — though infected and affected layers are hard to tell apart clinically.

Contemporary aims of restoration
  1. Aid biofilm control on a restored rather than cavitated surface
  2. Protect the pulp–dentine complex and arrest the lesion by sealing it with an adhesive material
  3. Restore function, form and aesthetics

The only evidence-based reason for (selective) removal: enough cavity volume and surface area for restoration bulk and bond, while keeping the tooth structure that supports it → longevity of the tooth–restoration complex.

Five guiding principles

Remove carious tissue only when there is no feasible alternative (e.g. regularly cleaning the cavity with brush and fluoride toothpaste — particularly suitable in primary teeth).

  1. Preserve non-demineralised and remineralisable tissue.
  2. Achieve an adequate peripheral seal on sound dentine and/or enamel.
  3. Avoid discomfort, pain and anxiety — ART, the Hall technique (primary teeth), chemomechanical agents (e.g. Carisolv gel).
  4. Maintain pulp health — avoid excavating close to the pulp; leave softer affected dentine there if required. Avoiding exposure significantly improves the tooth's lifetime prognosis and lowers long-term costs.
  5. Maximise longevity of the tooth–restoration complex — remove enough soft dentine for a restoration of sufficient bulk and resilience while keeping enough surrounding tooth to support it.

Balance (4) against (5): deep lesions (inner ⅓ or ¼ of dentine radiographically, or a risk of exposure) → pulp health; shallow/moderate → longevity (Fig 2).

How to manage each lesion type

LesionManagement
Non-cavitated, cleansableBiofilm disruption (brushing with fluoride toothpaste) ± topical remineralisation (high risk), or therapeutic fissure sealing (Fig 3)
Non-cavitated but radiographically extensive (occlusal)May not arrest with biofilm control → therapeutic sealant, monitored; soft dentine underneath may cause a "trampoline" failure → restore
Cavitated, accessiblePotentially cleansable by a motivated patient → inactivate non-operatively (oral hygiene, fluoride toothpaste, remineralisation)
Cavitated, non-cleansableLikely active. Can it be made cleansable? → non-restorative cavity control (primary teeth; advocated by G.V. Black in 1908), with fluoride varnish, remineralising agents or an HV-GIC layer. If not → operative care (Fig 4)

Clinical presentation of carious dentine
