Hardness levels are a continuous spectrum, not discrete layers. The most practical test is the force a sharp explorer needs to make a mark. (Banerjee's Figs 5 and 6 reproduce the ICCC lesion diagram and decision tree — topic 04.)

DentineFeelOften described as
SoftDeforms under a sharp probe with a latent "stickiness"; easily scooped; may look moistCaries-infected
LeatheryDoesn't deform but lifts easily; latent "tackiness"; a transition from soft to firmCaries-affected
FirmResists hand excavation; needs some pressure to lift—
HardNeeds a pushing force to engage; only a sharp edge or bur lifts it; "cri dentinaire"Classically sound

Removal strategies and methods

  • Outcome terms ("complete") have undefined criteria, no chairside test, and better technology would find residual tissue anyway — when to stop is arbitrary. Hence procedural terms: selective removal = periphery to sound enamel and hard dentine for the best adhesive seal; firm or leathery tissue left pulpally, removing only enough for a durable restoration while "avoiding pulp exposure at all costs". Strategy is chosen by lesion depth and activity.
  • Non-selective to hard = "gross over-treatment". Selective to firm = treatment of choice for shallow/moderate lesions in both dentitions. Selective to soft = deep lesions; significantly fewer exposures. Stepwise (permanent, deep): provisional lasting up to 12 months (e.g. HV-GIC), then removal to firm dentine that formed as the lesion arrested; the second stage may be omitted; not needed in primary teeth.
  • Methods: hand instruments, burs (tungsten carbide, ceramic, carbon-steel, polymer), air- or sono-abrasion, chemomechanical agents, lasers. Some evidence favours hand or chemomechanical removal for selective removal and less pain.
  • ART: hand instruments open small cavities and remove caries; the cavity and remaining pits and fissures are sealed with an adhesive material (usually HV-GIC) — selective to firm in small/medium cavities, to soft in deep ones.
  • Hall technique: a correctly sized preformed metal crown, filled with GI luting cement, seated firmly over a primary molar — no tissue removal, no local anaesthetic. Children preferred it in two RCTs; it outperformed conventional restorations and compares favourably with conventional crowns.
  • Cavity disinfection: bacteria matter little for progression or for CARS (caries associated with restorations and sealants = secondary/recurrent caries); no difference in restoration survival; adds time and cost.
  • Lining (Ca(OH)₂): antibacterial effect of limited relevance; remineralisation is pulp-cell mediated; evidence sparse. Thermal insulation matters under amalgam; under composite it may limit monomer penetration and dentine fracture (more evidence needed). Material: by location, extent, risk, activity and patient — no definitive evidence.
  • Changing practice is slow: knowledge is necessary but not sufficient — MI skills and the right attitude are needed, starting in dental schools with teachers trained in contemporary cariology.
The 10 summary recommendations
  1. Prevent lesions by managing the disease with the team and patient; control activity; avoid the destructive restorative cycle.
  2. Intervene operatively (minimally invasively) when a lesion is non-cleansable and sealing is no longer an option.
  3. Restorations aid biofilm control, protect the dentine–pulp complex and restore function, form and aesthetics. Removal creates a long-lasting tooth–restoration complex, preserves remineralisable tissue, seals and protects pulp health — preferably with low-anxiety methods.
  4. Deep lesions → pulp health over "mechanical" success; shallow/moderate → longevity.
  5. Shallow/moderate → selective removal to firm.
  6. Deep lesions (primary and permanent) → selective removal to soft.
  7. Permanent deep lesions → stepwise is also an option (the second stage may not be needed).
  8. Hardness is the primary criterion; no removal method is proven better.
  9. Cavity disinfection has no significant evidence base.
  10. No recommendation on restorative materials is possible yet.
Compare & contrast
Kidd 2004Banerjee 2017
RoleThe evidence and biological rationale (sealing beats removal; bacteria entombed)The ICCC consensus translated for practitioners, 13 years later
LanguageInfected/affected, "firm and leathery", complete vs incompleteICCC terms: selective removal to soft/firm, stepwise, non-selective
Stepwise re-entryAsks whether re-entry is neededAnswers: the second stage may be omitted
LinersCa(OH)₂ indirect pulp capping is still taughtNot needed to control a sealed lesion; evidence sparse
ExtrasDetector dyes unreliable; research agendaHall, ART, NRCC, chemomechanical; anxiety; education and remuneration barriers
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Kidd: draws together clinical, radiographic and microbiological evidence (sealants 1975–92, stepwise 1961–2002, four RCTs); candid about weak evidence; sets a research agenda. Its argument runs through the ICCC papers (Kidd presented at the meeting).
  • Banerjee: international consensus made practical, illustrated and readable for general dentists; patient-centred (anxiety, Hall, ART); tackles why practice is slow to change.
Limitations
  • Kidd: narrative, not systematic; studies small (some n = 4), old, mostly uncontrolled and short; microbiological counts are surrogates; Weerheijm's contrary findings; some cited studies are the author's own.
  • Banerjee: a re-written consensus by its own organisers — no new evidence, and the recommendation grades are dropped; hardness end points are subjective ("arbitrary"); evidence for NRCC (e.g. age to start) is limited; no material guidance; industry-sponsored meeting.
Clinical relevance
  • The seal at the periphery matters more than how "clean" the floor is: leave stain at a hard EDJ, and soft or leathery dentine over the pulp in deep lesions.
  • Don't use caries-detector dye; judge by hardness. Drier, harder, darker dentine = arrested.
  • Use low-anxiety methods (ART, Hall crowns on primary molars, chemomechanical gel); use NRCC when a primary-tooth cavity can be made cleansable.
  • Monitor sealed lesions and repair sealants to keep the seal.
Exam practice
SAQContrast the views of Tomes (1859) and Black (1908) on residual carious dentine.

Tomes: better to leave discoloured dentine to protect the pulp than risk losing the tooth. Black: better to expose the pulp than leave it covered only with softened dentine. Kidd's evidence and the ICCC support Tomes.

SAQSummarise the findings of studies placing sealants over carious dentine.

Sealed lesions arrested clinically and radiographically; bacteria fell sharply or disappeared (some S. mutans and lactobacilli survived); dentine looked drier; no pulpitis; progression only where sealants were lost or absent. Exception: Weerheijm 1992 (retrospective — active-looking dentine and cariogenic bacteria in 50% under intact sealants, but no baseline sample).

SAQWhat changes are seen at re-entry in stepwise excavation studies?

Dentine is drier, harder and darker (more radio-opaque); the cultivable flora is much smaller, sometimes sterile, and shifts to a less cariogenic flora (fewer lactobacilli and gram-negative rods; Actinomyces naeslundii and streptococci dominate). Exposures are fewer than with complete removal (15 vs 53%; 17.5 vs 40%).

SAQWhat did Mertz-Fairhurst 1998 show, and why is it important?

Soft, moist, infected dentine was left at the EDJ and over the pulp under bonded, sealed composites in occlusal lesions (n = 156, no re-entry). At 10 years the lesions had arrested, with no more failures than the amalgam controls. A durable seal, not complete removal, controls the lesion.

SAQWhy does Kidd say caries-detector dyes are unhelpful?

The dye does not discriminate bacterially infected dentine from softened affected dentine, so it leads to over-preparation at the EDJ and unnecessary removal over the pulp.

SAQDescribe the feel of soft and leathery dentine (Banerjee 2017).

Soft deforms under a sharp probe with a latent "stickiness", is scooped easily and may look moist (often called infected). Leathery doesn't deform but lifts easily, with a latent "tackiness" (often called affected).

SAQList the three contemporary aims of restoring a carious lesion.

(1) Aid biofilm control on a restored rather than cavitated surface; (2) protect the pulp–dentine complex and arrest the lesion by sealing it with an adhesive material; (3) restore function, form and aesthetics.

LAQ"How clean must a cavity be before restoration?" Answer using Kidd 2004 and Banerjee 2017, including the evidence and its limitations.
  1. Premise: biofilm activity drives mineral loss; a cavity shelters biofilm; restoration restores a cleansable surface and seals. So "clean" may be irrelevant — the seal matters.
  2. History: Tomes vs Black; "drill and fill".
  3. Evidence: sealants over caries (arrest, bacteria fall, no pulpitis; Weerheijm the outlier); stepwise (fewer exposures, 15 vs 53% and 17.5 vs 40%; re-entry dentine drier, harder, darker; less cariogenic flora); Mertz-Fairhurst 10 years; Ribeiro; detector dyes over-prepare.
  4. Translation (Banerjee): selective removal — periphery hard for the seal; firm pulpally (shallow/moderate) or soft (deep); stepwise with an optional second stage; Hall, ART, NRCC, chemomechanical; no disinfection; liners optional; hardness as the criterion.
  5. Limitations: small, old, mostly uncontrolled studies; surrogate microbiological outcomes; subjective hardness; consensus without new evidence; slow change in education and payment systems.
  6. Conclusion: clean enough at the periphery to bond and seal; no cleaner over the pulp than a durable restoration needs.
06

Tooth prognosis & restorative decision-making

  • No accepted, standardised system existed for the prognosis of an individual tooth. Samet & Jotkowitz built one from the literature plus a Delphi process: classes A, B, C, D and X.
  • Two phases: patient-level risk factors, then individual teeth — 4 criteria (periodontal support, restorability, endodontic condition, occlusal plane/position) + 2 compromising factors (anatomic, iatrogenic).
  • Bone support / sound coronal structure: 80–100% A · 50–80% B · 30–50% C · <30% D · X = non-salvageable (e.g. vertical root fracture, no supragingival tooth left).
  • Rules: the most severe single criterion sets the class → anatomic/iatrogenic factors drop one class → considerable patient-level risk drops every tooth one class (improvement can raise it again).
  • A relative, not absolute, prognosis: evidence on prognostic predictors is lacking, and the system itself is untested.
Samet & Jotkowitz 2009 · literature review + proposed classification

Classification and prognosis evaluation of individual teeth — a comprehensive approach

Quintessence Int 2009;40(5):377–387 · Harvard School of Dental Medicine
  • Prognosis = "a prediction of the probable course and outcome of a disease, and the likelihood of recovery from a disease".
  • Aims: a common language between professionals · medico-legal case evaluation · a baseline for assessing treatment outcomes · uniform evaluation by young and experienced clinicians · patient understanding and informed consent.
  • Like Angle's and Kennedy's classifications: simple but comprehensive, standardised and meaningful. Includes only criteria with a significant impact; assumes treatment follows current accepted standards.
  • Deliberately excludes the operator's skill and comfort zone, to keep the focus on the patient's condition.
  • The Delphi method gathered input from clinicians and specialists, so the system rests on evidence where available and on accepted best practice (17 specialists and faculty are acknowledged).

What the literature says

AreaFindings
Periodontal
  • Most attempts come from periodontology, but traditional systems measure tooth mortality (did it survive?), not whether a tooth suits a restorative plan.
  • Hirschfeld & Wasserman 1978 (22 years, 600 patients): favourable vs questionable (deep probing depth, furcation, bone loss, mobility). Critique: deep pockets show active disease, furcation and bone loss show past disease, and mobility may be occlusal.
  • Becker 1984: good / questionable / hopeless. Questionable = at least one of 50% bone loss, PD 6–8 mm, Class 2 furcation, or anatomic variables (deep palatal groove on maxillary incisors, mesial furcation of the maxillary first premolar). Hopeless = more than one of >75% bone loss, PD >8 mm, Class 3 furcation, Class 3 mobility, poor crown–root ratio, unfavourable root proximity, repeated abscesses. Accurate only in well-maintained patients.
  • McGuire & Nunn (100 patients, 5/8/15 years): clinical parameters predicted no outcome other than "good"; initial prognosis didn't adequately predict survival; IL-1 genotype and smoking improved accuracy (topic 07).
  • Muzzi 2006 (10 years, strict maintenance): the infrabony component and residual bone may predict loss; traditional measures of little value. Kwok & Caton 2007: prognosis by whether periodontal stability can be achieved; separates tooth from patient prognosis, but periodontal factors only.
Restorative
  • Success of root-filled teeth depends on the amount of remaining sound coronal structure; "tissue preservation" is the most critical aspect; an adequate ferrule is accepted. Problem: it has to be judged before caries removal.
  • Bandlish 2006 tooth restorability index: the tooth divided into sextants, each scored 0–3 (none / inadequate / questionable / adequate dentine) → maximum 18; "moderate to good" agreement between 3 dentists scoring casts of 20 teeth. Other approaches are subjective.
Endodontic
  • Prognosis is linked to case difficulty (calcification, isolation, resorption, extra roots/canals, retreatment, posts, ledges, perforations) — UCSF, AAE, Canadian and Dutch difficulty guides.
  • A periapical radiolucency lowers success; finding its cause is key.
  • Crowning root-filled teeth is strongly associated with survival; endodontics isn't complete until the coronal restoration is placed; the coronal seal is at least as important as the apical seal.
Occlusal plane
  • No literature defines how much super-eruption or tipping makes a tooth non-salvageable.
  • Accepted: restore teeth to the correct plane; over-erupted or tilted teeth can block function and complicate restoring the opposing arch. Options: enameloplasty, orthodontics, partial or full coverage, endo + crown lengthening + restoration, extraction — watch the crown–root ratio. Segmental jaw surgery is excluded.

Phase 1 — patient-level risk factors (Table 1)

CategoryExamples
BiologicMedical conditions impairing immunity or healing · impaired salivary flow · disability limiting oral hygiene · high S. mutans/Lactobacillus counts · IL-1 genotype positive · family history · other missing teeth
BehaviouralPoor oral hygiene · cariogenic diet · low fluoride exposure · parafunction · ability and willingness to keep up maintenance · smoking
Financial / personalMotivation · resources · willingness to commit money, time and effort · attitude to losing teeth · understanding of the condition · aesthetic expectations · low dental IQ
  • A further factor: the quality of dental treatment and of maintenance. Assess with caries (CAMBRA) and periodontal risk tools, which group patients as high, medium or low risk.
  • Divide factors into modifiable and non-modifiable; reassess prognosis once modifiable ones are managed; flag them in the chart. Multiple non-modifiable or uncontrolled factors → an inferior case prognosis.
  • Aesthetics drive treatment choice but don't alter tooth prognosis (they may lead to extracting a savable tooth).

Phase 2 — the five classes (Table 2)

ClassPeriodontalRestorativeEndodonticOcclusal / position
A · Good
minimal risk of loss		80–100% bone support; easily maintained80–100% sound coronal structure; easily restoredStraightforward primary RCT, or existing good RCTCorrect plane, or slight deviation (minimal enameloplasty)
B · Fair
predictable, low risk		50–80%; maintainable with rigorous therapy; defects/furcations treatable to cleansable or by predictable regeneration; molars at higher risk than single-rooted teeth50–80%; involved procedures but no biologic-width infringement, adequate ferrule, good crown–root ratioFailing RCT with an obvious cause, predictably retreatable; or a difficult primary RCTOut of plane but adjustable (may need exposed dentine sealed)
C · Questionable
medium risk		30–50%; no acute outbreaks, but cleansability hard to maintain; needs therapy and thorough maintenance30–50%; or a ferrule only by compromising crown–root ratio or adjacent structuresAcute or chronic failing RCT that is difficult to retreat predictablyOut of plane, needing multiple procedures
D · Compromised
high risk		<30% and/or can't be cleansed or maintained, with active disease<30%; or no good ferrule without totally compromising support or crown–root ratioFailing RCT that cannot be predictably retreatedSo far out of plane or tilted that the crown–root ratio will be poor after extensive treatment, or it harms adjacent structures
X · Non-salvageable
extract		<30% and can't be cleansed or maintained without acute outbreaksNo supragingival sound structure; loss deep into root dentine or canalsVertical root fracture; or retreated several times (orthograde/surgical) without resolutionSo super-erupted or tilted it can't be restored to function, or blocks restoring the same or opposing arch

Class D has no pathology demanding immediate extraction, but investing in it may not be in the patient's interest — external and patient factors decide. Class X can't be restored, or has pathology dentistry can't solve, and may endanger the patient's health.

The classification rules

  1. Step 1 — the 4 criteria. Grade each independently, on the present condition and the expected status after caries removal. The single most severe criterion determines the class.
  2. Step 2 — anatomic / iatrogenic factors drop one class (Table 3); more than two such findings may drop it further. Anatomic: irregular, multiple, thin, short or very conical roots. Iatrogenic: perforations, extensive post preparations, minimal tooth thickness after preparation, materials that can't be removed — with no active pathology the tooth may still be fair or good, but it drops if further treatment is planned or other signs appear.
  3. Step 3 — considerable patient-level risk drops every tooth one class. Reassess over time: lower the class if modifiable factors don't change (or significant non-modifiable ones are present); raise it with an obvious improvement.

Discussion points

  • Treatment planning is multi-stage: manage the cause, monitor, treat mechanically or surgically, then maintain long term. Sometimes the extent of caries is known only after removal (CAMBRA helps judge progression).
  • A planned abutment that turns out Class C or D → consider an alternative plan. Teeth restored as single units may still be kept as an interim solution if that fits the patient's goals and finances.
  • Reported outcome: well received at expert peer review; Harvard students using it gave realistic prognoses more accurately and promptly than their predecessors and planned better — no data presented.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Comprehensive: perio, restorative, endo, occlusal, anatomic, iatrogenic and patient factors in one system.
  • Simple letter grades → a common language; teaching, consent and medico-legal value.
  • Dynamic: reassessed over time; modifiable vs non-modifiable risk; links to CAMBRA and perio risk tools.
  • Candid that prognosis is relative and the evidence limited.
Limitations
  • Not validated — no reliability or outcome data; the student benefit is anecdotal.
  • The Delphi process isn't described (panel, rounds, consensus threshold).
  • The 80/50/30% cut-offs are arbitrary and hard to measure clinically.
  • "Most severe criterion" ignores cumulative problems; drop rules are subjective; D and X periodontal criteria both use <30%, separated by acute outbreaks.
  • Excludes operator skill, which the authors admit affects outcome.
Contrasting viewpoints
  • McGuire & Nunn (topic 07): prognoses other than "good" were poor predictors — any grading system needs outcome testing.
  • Hirschfeld & Wasserman (topic 08): many teeth of questionable prognosis were kept for decades with maintenance — a caution against condemning C and D teeth early.
Clinical relevance
  • Grade every tooth before committing to complex treatment, especially abutments; plans built on C or D teeth need alternatives.
  • Use the class to explain prognosis and record consent.
  • Address modifiable patient factors first (smoking, hygiene, diet, parafunction), then re-grade.
Exam practice
SAQList the four main criteria and two additional factors in the Samet & Jotkowitz system.

Main: (1) periodontal condition and alveolar bone support; (2) restorability (remaining sound tooth structure); (3) endodontic condition; (4) occlusal plane and tooth position. Additional: anatomic irregularities and iatrogenic compromising factors.

SAQDescribe the three steps used to assign a class.

(1) Grade each of the 4 criteria (now and after caries removal); the most severe single one sets the class. (2) Anatomic or iatrogenic factors drop it one class (more than two may drop it further). (3) Considerable patient-level risk drops all teeth one class; reassess over time (up with clear improvement, down if nothing changes).

SAQWhat distinguishes a Class D from a Class X tooth?

D = compromised, high risk, but no pathology demands immediate extraction; investing may not be in the patient's interest, so patient and external factors decide (e.g. <30% support or structure, failing RCT that can't be predictably retreated). X = non-salvageable → extract: vertical root fracture, no supragingival sound structure, repeated failed retreatment, <30% support with acute outbreaks, or a position that blocks restoration.

SAQWhy did the authors criticise Hirschfeld & Wasserman's "questionable" criteria?

They mix a marker of active disease (deep pockets) with markers of past disease (furcation involvement, bone loss), and mobility may be occlusal rather than periodontal.

SAQGive three limitations of the classification.

Not validated (no reliability or outcome data); arbitrary, hard-to-measure percentage cut-offs; Delphi process not described; the most-severe rule ignores cumulative effects; subjective drop rules; student benefit is anecdotal.

LAQDiscuss how you would determine the prognosis of an individual tooth before restorative treatment planning, using Samet & Jotkowitz and the other prognosis papers.
  1. Why it matters: communication, consent, medico-legal records, avoiding failed complex treatment (especially abutments).
  2. Patient level first: biologic, behavioural and financial/personal factors; CAMBRA and periodontal risk tools; modifiable vs non-modifiable; control what can change.
  3. Tooth level: perio (bone %, furcations, cleansability), restorability (sound structure %, ferrule, biologic width, crown–root ratio — judged after caries removal), endo (difficulty, cause of failure, retreatability, VRF), occlusal position; then the A–X bands and 3 steps.
  4. Evidence: McGuire & Nunn — clinical prognoses reliable only for "good" teeth; smoking and IL-1 matter. H&W — questionable teeth often survive with maintenance. Becker — accuracy only in maintained patients.
  5. Appraisal and conclusion: a useful common language but unvalidated and subjective; prognosis is relative and should be re-graded after initial therapy and over time.
07

Prognosis accuracy & concurrent endo-perio disease

  • McGuire & Nunn: a model built from the commonly taught clinical parameters predicted the 5- and 8-year prognosis of 81% of teeth — but about 70% of teeth were "good". For teeth worse than good, accuracy was 43% (5 y) and 35% (8 y): "a coin toss would be an easier and more accurate way".
  • Smoking cut the odds of improvement by ~60% (OR 0.418) and doubled worsening (OR 1.90); controlled diabetes doubled worsening (2.09); endodontic involvement OR 3.87; good hygiene improved (OR 2.50).
  • Probing depth, furcation and mobility reflect disease that has already progressed. Crown-to-root ratio, malposition, smoking and fixed-abutment status are known when the prognosis is assigned → weight these more.
  • Abbott: only two categories — concurrent endodontic and periodontal diseases without or with communication. Without → endo first, perio soon after. With → medicate the canal (Ledermix → 50:50 with Ca(OH)₂ at 4 weeks), start perio, reassess at 3 months, then root-fill.
  • Root planing removes cementum and opens tubules; an infected canal impairs periodontal healing → remove the intracanal infection before any cementum is removed.
Paper 1 · McGuire & Nunn 1996 · retrospective cohort, private practice

Prognosis versus actual outcome. II. The effectiveness of clinical parameters in developing an accurate prognosis

J Periodontol 1996;67(7):658–665 · periodontal practice, Houston · University of Washington (biostatistics)
  • Risk factor = a characteristic associated with developing the disease. Prognostic factor = predicts the outcome once disease is present, without causing it.
  • Prognosis methods are handed down from one generation to the next without evidence; idiosyncratic judgement and subjective variables can lead clinicians to overestimate an approach. Unbiased quantitative data improve accuracy.
  • Part I (McGuire 1991): the fate of "hopeless" teeth varied widely; individual prognoses changed often; the usual factors predicted nothing but "good" well; prognoses were more accurate for single-rooted than multi-rooted teeth.
  • Method: 100 consecutive patients with ≥5 years' maintenance, from one clinician's appointment book; chronic generalised moderate–severe adult periodontitis, treated by the same clinician; 2- or 3-month recall ("well maintained"). 2,484 teeth over 5 years (38 patients over 8). Prognosis assigned after active therapy, then reassigned at 5 and 8 years from the charted data by the same examiner, blind to earlier assessments. Generalised estimating equations (teeth clustered within patients); multiple linear and logistic regression; 5-year models tested on 8-year data.

Prognosis definitions (Table 2)

PrognosisDefinition
GoodAetiology controlled and adequate support; relatively easy to maintain
Fair~25% attachment loss and/or Class I furcation; maintainable with good compliance
Poor50% attachment loss with Class II furcations; maintainable, but with difficulty
Questionable>50% attachment loss → poor crown-to-root ratio; poor root form; Class II furcations not easily accessible, or Class III; mobility 2+ or more; significant root proximity
HopelessInadequate attachment to maintain the tooth; extraction performed or suggested

Commonly taught factors (Table 1) — tooth: % bone loss, deepest probing depth, horizontal/vertical loss, furcation, mobility, crown-to-root ratio, root form, caries/pulpal involvement, malposition, abutment status; overall: age, smoking/diabetes, family history, hygiene, compliance, maintenance interval, parafunction ± biteguard.

Results

Initial prognosis was worse with greater probing depth, furcation involvement, mobility, unfavourable crown-to-root ratio, malposition and fixed-abutment status (the final regression model).

Model accuracy (prognosis predicted correctly)5 years8 years
All teeth81% (2,007 teeth)81% (751 teeth)
Predicted worse / better than recorded5% / 14%4% / 15%
Anteriors · non-molars · molars89% · 87% · 65%92% · 87% · 65%
Teeth worse than "good"43%35%
… molars · anteriors · non-molars59% · 28% · 23%47% · 4% · 21%

Molars did better than other teeth once "good" teeth were excluded — probably because more anteriors were excluded as good, and factors like furcation apply mainly to molars.

Hygiene and mobility not significant for worsening. Sensitivity 67%, specificity 76% (8 y: 66%, 60%).

  • Under maintenance, compromised teeth tended to improve or hold: poor and questionable teeth were ~7.5 and ~12 times as likely to improve as fair ones, and fair and poor teeth only 17% and 2% as likely to worsen as good ones.
  • Hygiene and mobility may not have affected worsening because such teeth were already given worse prognoses, or because professional maintenance offset poor home care.

Discussion

  • Traditional prognosis rests on an outdated disease model (all plaque the same, everyone equally susceptible, host ignored). The new paradigm: site-specific infections depending on pathogens, protective species and host resistance.
  • Ghiai & Bissada's model was 38% successful, with mobility the most important factor — mobility summarises attachment loss, occlusal stability and parafunction.
  • Probing depth, furcation and mobility only appear after the disease has progressed, so they make poor predictors. Crown-to-root ratio, malposition, smoking and fixed-abutment status are available when the prognosis is assigned and deserve more weight.
  • Population: 40% had parafunction (only 40% of those wore biteguards); hygiene good 20%, fair 66%, poor 14%. Very compliant (non-compliers had dropped out) → results apply to well-maintained patients, like Hirschfeld & Wasserman's.
  • Authors' caveats: retrospective (records, patient memory); the examiner knew which factors patients had (though not which mattered); prognosis is not a true end-point — tooth loss is.
  • Conclusion: clinical parameters alone are "surprisingly accurate" overall, but the traditional approach is ineffective for teeth below "good" — the teeth that most need a prognosis. Clear, objective criteria are needed.
Paper 2 · Abbott & Castro Salgado 2009 · review + new classification + protocol

Strategies for the endodontic management of concurrent endodontic and periodontal diseases

Aust Dent J 2009;54(1 Suppl):S70–S85 · School of Dentistry, University of Western Australia

The biology

  • Both diseases are bacterial infections with similar, complex flora. An untreated infection in one tissue can cause signs in the other, and cross-seeding can occur in either direction.
  • Concurrent disease is harder to diagnose and manage, the prognosis is less predictable, and patients may not commit to the cost and time. Terminology has been confusing, with little research in the last decade.
Pulpal disease with periodontal signs
  • A chronic apical abscess draining via the sulcus mimics a deep, narrow pocket; accessory canals can give a furcation radiolucency. Occurs in pulpless infected or previously root-filled teeth (Fig 3).
  • Irreversible pulpitis rarely, if ever, causes periodontal or bony defects (except "pulp necrobiosis" — one canal pulpitic, another infected).
  • Find the cause of necrosis (caries, crack, marginal breakdown, trauma); record the sinus or defect so its healing can be checked.
Periodontal disease affecting the pulp
  • Pulpitis, secondary dentine or internal resorption only when pockets reach lateral canals or tubules of exposed root dentine; complete necrosis only if the pocket reaches the main apical foramen.
  • Root planing can cause reversible pulpitis (cold, occasionally hot; pain lasts seconds; resolves in 1–2 weeks), occasionally irreversible.
  • A deep pocket past the apex can mimic a periapical lesion (Fig 4) → sensibility testing is essential. No cause of necrosis and no entry pathway → suspect a pocket.

Existing classifications — and why they fail

ClassificationBasisCritique
Simon 1972 (modified by Gargiulo 1984)5 groups: primary endo; primary endo + secondary perio; primary perio; primary perio + secondary endo; "true combined"The "primary" lesions are single-site diseases, not combined ones. You can't tell which tissue was affected first, so "secondary" and "true combined" can't be separated.
WeineTreatment needsUnacceptable — diagnose before deciding treatment; needs vary within one disease.
GuldenerCause + treatment needs, including perforations, resorption, fractures, groovesToo broad — these have their own causes and protocols, and aren't all diseases (diagnose "an infected vertical root fracture…", not an endo-perio lesion).
Torabinejad & TropeOrigin of the pocket: endodontic, periodontal, combined (with or without communication)The first two are single-site; a later edition of the textbook reverted to Simon.

The new classification — "concurrent endodontic and periodontal diseases"

Only teeth with both diseases at once: an infected canal with apical periodontitis plus marginal periodontitis with pocketing — two independent processes (relatively uncommon; no incidence data). Initially separate, they may meet if left to progress.

Diagnosis

  • Endodontic: sensibility tests + radiographs. A periapical radiolucency is reliable evidence of an infected canal — but radiographic signs lag (2–4 months, sometimes over 10, in a monkey study), and a radiolucency may be unrelated to the pulp.
  • Periodontal: probing + radiographs. A wide-based, cone-shaped defect — the probe "steps down" then "steps up" — unlike the deep, narrow defect of a sinus tract or an infected root crack. Bone loss usually on several teeth (several infected canals at once is uncommon).
  • Usually symptomless unless an acute apical or periodontal abscess develops.
  • Use history, sensibility tests (ideally thermal and electric), probing, palpation, percussion, mobility, transillumination and removing existing restorations. Sensibility tests show nerve response, not blood supply; calcification, root fillings, pulpotomies and porcelain crowns give false results. Take parallel radiographs with beam-guiding holders. A root filling that looks good can still contain bacteria.
Typical finding (Table 1)Pulp / periapicalPeriodontalConcurrent
Localised to one toothYesNoYes*
Extensive caries / restorationsYesNoYes
Responds to sensibility testsNoYesNo
Probing defectNo (deep, narrow if a sinus exits in the sulcus)Deep, wide-basedDeep, wide-based
Crestal bone lossNoYesYes
Periapical radiolucency / lamina dura lossYesNoYes
Tender to percussion / palpationNo — unless acute (apical or periodontal abscess); chronic disease may "feel different"

*More teeth may be involved if periodontitis is generalised.

Evidence that decides the sequence

  • Flora: similar, but spirochaetes are 30–60% of pocket flora vs 0–10% in infected canals; pockets hold more species; canals in concurrent disease have a more complex flora.
  • Jaoui 1995: over 8 years after periodontal treatment, 6% of 195 root-filled teeth were extracted vs none of 521 teeth with normal pulps.
  • Lindskog 1993: healing against cementum favours connective tissue; against dentine, rapid epithelial down-growth (long junctional epithelium).
  • Jansson & Ehnevid studies (monkeys, periodontitis-prone patients): infected canals → deeper pockets, more attachment loss, more radiographic loss over 6 years — a risk factor at least as large as an overhanging restoration; more resorption where cementum was removed; less pocket reduction after non-surgical treatment. Endodontic infection should get priority in periodontitis-prone patients.
  • Root fillings don't seal completely (over 150 apical penetration studies) → bacteria from a communicating pocket can re-infect the canal, so keep it medicated during periodontal treatment.
  • Intracanal medication is essential — routine one-visit endodontics isn't supported. Byström: filing and irrigation reduce but don't eliminate bacteria. Teeth with no bacteria at root filling healed 26% (Sjögren 1997) and 47% (Sundqvist 1998) more often.
MedicamentActionsDrawbacks
Ledermix (corticosteroid–antibiotic paste)Antibacterial; anti-inflammatory (fewer symptoms); corticosteroid inhibits clastic cells (less external inflammatory resorption); tetracycline inhibits osteoclasts, binds to tooth and bone (stays in place) and inhibits collagenase—
Calcium hydroxideAntibacterial; stimulates hard-tissue repairWorks through toxicity (surface necrosis) — may start or worsen external inflammatory resorption where cementum is missing or root-planed; long-term use → more ankylosis and replacement resorption; doesn't kill all bacteria
50:50 Ledermix + Ca(OH)₂ (e.g. Pulpdent)Less toxic than Ca(OH)₂ alone with a broader antibacterial spectrum than Ledermix alone — the second dressing in the protocol

Management

Acute first: acute apical abscess → start endo; acute periodontal abscess → start perio. Most cases are chronic and symptomless.

Without communication — endo first
  1. Clean, irrigate and medicate; root-fill aseptically; restore with correct contours (no overhangs or food traps).
  2. Periodontal treatment soon after, once the canal is free of bacteria.

Why: root planing removes cementum → exposed tubules let canal bacteria and endotoxins reach the PDL → delayed healing, external inflammatory resorption, epithelial down-growth, more bone loss and deeper pockets.

With communication — staged, concurrent
  1. Start endo under rubber dam: remove restorations, caries and cracks → assess restorability (extract now if unsuitable). Clean, irrigate, Ledermix; interim GIC ± steel band that doesn't hinder periodontal care.
  2. At 4 weeks: change to 50:50 Ledermix/Ca(OH)₂, then start perio (root planing + OHI ± surgical access) while the canal is medicated.
  3. Reassess at 3 months. Favourable → root-fill + coronal restoration → maintenance and periapical review.
  4. Not favourable → re-medicate + further perio → review after 3 months; keep re-medicating 3-monthly, or extract if the periodontal prognosis is poor. Before root resection or hemisection, complete the root filling.
  5. Defer cast crowns until reviews confirm the prognosis (meanwhile, e.g. an amalgam core with cusp overlay).
  • Ledermix first also arrests external inflammatory resorption, present in up to 80% of teeth with apical periodontitis.
  • Masquerading conditions: periodontal disease causing pulp changes → conventional perio first, review, and endo only if pulp symptoms persist; repeat sensibility tests at reviews (repeated insults → fibrosis → necrosis possible). A chronic apical abscess draining via the PDL should heal with endo; if not → periapical surgery (ideally at root filling); if still not → periodontal management.
  • Essentials: rubber dam for every phase including the final restoration; remove the cause (caries, cracks, fractures, broken restorations) first; a sealed interim restoration that doesn't irritate the gingiva; disinfection by debridement, irrigation and inter-appointment medication.
  • Review every endodontically treated tooth at 6–12 months, then every 3–4 years.
  • Prognosis can't be judged well before treatment — reassess after each phase. It depends on the primary cause, pre-treatment attachment loss, healing response, oral hygiene, compliance, maintenance and restoration longevity. The periodontal prognosis and the patient's oral hygiene are the main determinants; communicating disease has the worst prognosis. Don't condemn teeth quickly — provide the initial phases first.
Compare & contrast
McGuire & Nunn 1996Abbott & Castro Salgado 2009
QuestionHow accurate are periodontal prognoses?How should teeth with both diseases be diagnosed and sequenced?
EvidenceQuantitative retrospective cohort, one practiceNarrative review, animal studies, case reports, expert protocol
Endo involvementOR 3.87 for worseningAn infected canal impairs periodontal healing → treat the canal first
Key determinantsSmoking, diabetes, malposition, crown-to-root ratio, hygienePeriodontal prognosis and oral hygiene; communication or not
Shared messagePrognosis is uncertain and must be reassessed over time; don't condemn teeth prematurely.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • McGuire: 2,484 teeth over 5–8 years; blind reassessment; statistics suited to clustered teeth; models tested on 8-year data; challenges dogma with data.
  • Abbott: a simple, diagnosis-based classification; a staged protocol grounded in biology (cementum, tubules, flora, leakage); a differential-diagnosis table; cases followed for years.
Limitations
  • McGuire: retrospective; one clinician and practice; highly compliant patients only; prognosis is a surrogate for tooth loss; model tested on its own patients; examiner not fully naive; no microbial or host factors.
  • Abbott: low-level evidence (case reports, animal studies, opinion); no incidence data; the protocol reflects the authors' own medicament research (Ledermix); not tested in trials.
Clinical relevance
  • Treat a prognosis as provisional: reassess after initial therapy and at maintenance — especially for molars and teeth below "good".
  • Weight factors visible at baseline (smoking, crown-to-root ratio, malposition, abutment status) and tackle the modifiable ones (smoking, diabetes control, hygiene).
  • For any deep defect: sensibility-test, probe its shape (narrow vs wide), take parallel radiographs, and look for bone between pocket and apex.
  • Infected canal + periodontitis → canal first (medicated) before root planing; with communication, delay the root filling until the 3-month reassessment.
Exam practice
SAQDistinguish a risk factor from a prognostic factor.

A risk factor is associated with developing the disease in the first place. A prognostic factor predicts the outcome once disease is present, without causing it.

SAQMcGuire & Nunn reported 81% accuracy. Why is that figure misleading?

About 70% of teeth were initially "good", and good teeth tend to stay good. Excluding them, accuracy was only 43% at 5 years and 35% at 8 years (molars 65% overall) — a coin toss would do as well for compromised teeth, the ones that most need a prognosis.

SAQWhich factors significantly increased the odds of a tooth's prognosis worsening?

Endodontic involvement (OR 3.87), malposition (2.32), controlled diabetes (2.09), smoking (1.90), furcation (1.84), root form (1.61), probing depth (1.59 per mm). Fair and poor teeth were less likely to worsen than good ones (OR 0.168 and 0.023).

SAQDescribe Abbott's two categories of concurrent endodontic and periodontal disease.

Without communication — apical periodontitis and marginal periodontitis that don't meet: the probe doesn't reach the apical lesion and bone is visible between them. With communication — the pocket reaches the periapical lesion: one radiolucency with no bone between.

SAQWhy should root canal treatment precede root planing in concurrent disease?

Root planing removes cementum and exposes tubules, so bacteria and endotoxins from an infected canal can reach the periodontium → delayed healing, epithelial down-growth, external inflammatory resorption, deeper pockets. Healing against cementum favours connective tissue (Lindskog), and infected canals act as a periodontal risk factor (Jansson/Ehnevid).

SAQOutline the medicament sequence and timeline for a tooth with communicating endo-perio disease.

Ledermix at the first visit → at 4 weeks change to 50:50 Ledermix/Ca(OH)₂ and start periodontal therapy → reassess at 3 months → root-fill if favourable (otherwise re-medicate and repeat perio, or extract) → defer cast crowns → review at 6–12 months, then every 3–4 years.

LAQA patient has a deep periodontal defect on a heavily restored lower molar. Discuss diagnosis, prognosis and management, referring to McGuire & Nunn and Abbott & Castro Salgado.
  1. Diagnosis: history; sensibility tests (thermal + electric); probe the defect's shape (narrow = sinus or crack; wide = periodontal); percussion, palpation, mobility; transillumination; remove restorations to check for cracks; parallel periapicals (bone between pocket and apex?). Classify: endo, perio, or concurrent with/without communication.
  2. Prognosis: molar + endodontic involvement + furcation → worsening is more likely (endo OR 3.87), and prognoses for molars and teeth below "good" are unreliable. Patient factors: smoking, diabetes, hygiene. Communicating disease has the worst prognosis; the periodontal prognosis and hygiene dominate.
  3. Management: acute first; endo first (rubber dam, cleaning, Ledermix); without communication → root-fill then perio soon after; with communication → 50:50 at 4 weeks + perio, reassess at 3 months, then root-fill; defer the crown; maintain; review at 6–12 months.
  4. Critique and conclusion: McGuire is retrospective, single-practice, with prognosis as a surrogate; Abbott's evidence is low-level. Reassess at every phase and don't condemn the tooth prematurely.
08

Long-term tooth loss & periodontal risk assessment

  • Hirschfeld & Wasserman: 600 treated, maintained patients, mean 22 years: 7.1% of teeth lost to periodontal disease (1,110 of 15,666); 300 patients lost none.
  • Response groups: well-maintained 499 (lost 0–3) · downhill 76 (4–9) · extreme downhill 25 (10–23). Questionable teeth lost: 17.1% / 64.7% / 88.4% — one-sixth of patients lost most of them.
  • Maxillary molars had the worst prognosis and mandibular canines the best — no canines were lost in the well-maintained group. Loss was bilaterally symmetrical, and retention related more to case type than to surgery.
  • Lang & Tonetti (PRA): six vectors on a hexagon — BOP (<10% low, >25% high) · pockets ≥5 mm (≤4, >8) · teeth lost of 28 (≤4, >8) · bone loss/age (0.5, 1.0) · systemic/genetic (present = high) · smoking (heavy = high).
  • Overall: low = all low or one moderate · moderate = ≥2 moderate and ≤1 high · high = ≥2 high. Used to set the frequency and content of supportive periodontal therapy (SPT).
Paper 1 · Hirschfeld & Wasserman 1978 · retrospective long-term survey, private practice

A long-term survey of tooth loss in 600 treated periodontal patients

J Periodontol 1978;49(5):225–237 · Columbia University · aim: keep as many teeth as possible in health, function and comfort

Design and sample

  • 600 patients treated ≥15 years earlier, taken consecutively from the daily lists of a private practice and re-charted (1966–71); only cases with inadequate records were rejected. Untreated controls were impossible in clinical practice.
  • Maintenance every 4–6 months; mean 22 years (median 20, range 15–53). Mean age at treatment 42 (83% under 50); 65% female (no sex difference in severity); mostly Caucasian, middle-income, well motivated.
  • Initial severity: advanced 76.5% (pockets >7 mm, furcation involvement) · intermediate 16.5% (4–7 mm) · early 7% (≤4 mm).
  • "Questionable" tooth = ≥1 of: furcation involvement, a deep non-eradicable pocket (7–10 mm depending on root length), extensive bone loss, marked mobility with pocketing. Teeth lost during initial treatment weren't counted; later losses were assumed periodontal unless records said caries or periapical disease.
  • Treatment (all active treatment before 1956): subgingival scaling (older cases without LA) + selective grinding; later gingivectomy, osteoplasty, small flaps, infrabony procedures; root amputation/hemisection on only 17 teeth. Many deep pockets were simply accepted.
  • Recall: deep scaling, compare mobility and pocket depths, re-treat problem areas, adjust the occlusion. Oral hygiene: a modified Charters technique with a hard brush (Bass, scrub or a powered brush if ineffective). Some patients in every group had heavy plaque and calculus.
  • Mobility: residual mobility did not seem to cause further loss; increasing mobility → selective grinding, night guards or splinting; some mobile questionable teeth were kept unsplinted for years.

Results

After initial treatment, 75% of patients had more than 24 teeth (15,666 teeth in all). Over 22 years: 1,110 teeth (7.1%) were lost to periodontal disease and 202 (1.2%) for other reasons — 1.8 teeth per patient.

Response groupPatientsTeeth lost / patientTeeth lostLost teeth that were questionable

300 of the 499 well-maintained patients — half the whole sample — lost no teeth. The downhill groups lost proportionally more teeth that had been judged favourable.

Teeth lost, by groupWMDEDAll
Questionable (Table 10)272/1,592 · 17.1%249/385 · 64.7%145/164 · 88.4%666 of ~2,140 · 31%
Furcation-involved (Table 11)220/1,140 · 19.3%165/236 · 69.9%75/88 · ~85%460/1,464 · 31.4%
