Lost after surgery (Table 15)14.2%30.8%63.3%18.8%
  • Of the 666 questionable teeth lost, 394 were lost by one-sixth of the patients (D + ED) and only 272 by the other five-sixths. Of 460 furcated teeth lost, 240 were lost by the one-sixth who deteriorated most.
  • Well-maintained group: only 18.5% of furcated maxillary first and mandibular first and second molars were lost (maxillary second molars 23.6%); only 16.6% of furcated lower molars → safer to keep and use as abutments than previously believed. In D + ED, only 37 of 112 furcated lower molars survived.
  • Non-furcated questionable teeth (WM): none of 37 questionable canines lost; maxillary incisors 8.2% vs mandibular incisors 17.2%.

Order of loss (WM, Table 9): max 7 → max 6 → mand 7 → mand 6 → max 5 → mand 1 → max 4 → mand 5 → max 1 → max 2 → mand 4 → mand 2 → max 3 → mand 3 (most resistant). "Maxillary molars have the worst prognosis and lower cuspids the best." Third molars were also lost for non-periodontal reasons.

Other findings

  • Bilateral symmetry of disease and loss, as in Miller & Seidler, Wasserman & Geiger and others. The cause is unclear — tooth and housing anatomy, forces, local flora, "genetic keying".
  • Surgery: 230 patients (39%) had surgery — 36% of WM and about half of D and ED, where more areas were treated, mostly during maintenance because of poor progress. About 16% of each group had surgery during initial treatment, so initial involvement was similar. 102 areas were operated twice, 4× more often in the mandible. Lower canines and premolars survived surgery best. → Retention related more to case type than to the surgery performed.
  • Prostheses: half the distal-extension partial dentures in WM survived without splinting or crowned abutments; extensive splinting was far more common in D and ED (ED: 18 of 50 arches extensively splinted, 12 with complete dentures).
  • Inflammation ≠ destruction: many WM patients had plaque and gingivitis for years without losing bone or teeth. "Clinically evident inflammatory changes of the gingiva, though considered a precursor of periodontal destruction, may not necessarily evolve into a periodontal destructive lesion" (Wasserman & Geiger).
  • Host susceptibility: the groups had similar initial disease, questionable teeth and initial surgery — the only difference was more prior loss of first molars in ED (48% vs 28% maxillary / 35% mandibular in WM) — yet their courses were dramatically different.
  • Cyclic disease: irregular bursts of destruction in all groups; some advanced cases were stable for 20+ years, then broke down rapidly. Maintenance didn't prevent the loss of 70 originally normal teeth in WM (20.5% of WM losses).
  • Simple but thorough care (subgingival scaling, occlusal adjustment, fair-to-good home care) reduced loss in the great majority. In D and ED, surgery, splinting and better hygiene only delayed loss. Periodic deep scaling may disturb the subgingival ecosystem for a long time (Socransky; Listgarten).
  • Untreated comparison (Marshall-Day's cross-sectional survey of 1,187 people): from age 40–45 to 60–65, 10 more teeth were missing vs 2.2 here (5.9 at 42 → 8.1 at 64) — about 5× less loss with treatment; at 64, 25% vs 60% of teeth lost. The authors caution against firm conclusions (different designs and populations).
  • vs Oliver (mean 10 years, 1.6% loss): H&W followed patients longer and kept more questionable teeth (9.3% furcated at the start — nearly twice Oliver's), so more were lost overall (7.1%; WM 2.6%).
Paper 2 · Lang & Tonetti 2003 · conceptual risk tool

Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) for patients in supportive periodontal therapy (SPT)

Oral Health Prev Dent 2003;1(1):7–16 · University of Berne & Eastman Dental Institute, London · funded by the Swiss National Foundation

Rationale

  • The status after successful active therapy is a new baseline. Stability is a dynamic equilibrium between bacterial challenge and host response, so the multilevel risk profile must be monitored continuously and recall timed by overall risk.
  • All maintenance patients are at moderate-to-high risk because of their history; without recall, attachment loss progresses (Axelsson & Lindhe; Becker; Cortellini). Risk-based preventive care is very cost-effective and prevents both under- and over-treatment.
  • No single parameter is paramount, so all are assessed together on a functional diagram — one vector per factor, each with low-, moderate- and high-risk zones.
  • Compliance: only a minority comply with SPT; non-compliers are at higher risk (non-attenders had more stressful life events and less stable relationships). Plaque: the main aetiological agent; 20–40% plaque-covered surfaces may be tolerable for most patients — relate it to the host response. Neither is a vector.

The six vectors

VectorScaleLowModerateHighRationale
1 · BOP (% of sites)Quadratic: 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ≥49<10%10–25%>25%Objective inflammation measure summarising plaque control, host response and compliance. 25% separated stable from recurrent patients over 4 years (Joss 1994); 20–30% in other studies.
2 · Residual pockets ≥5 mm (number)Linear: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ≥12≤45–8>8Reflects treatment success; with BOP or suppuration they are ecological niches for reinfection.
3 · Tooth loss (of 28; third molars excluded)Linear: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ≥12≤45–8>8A true end-point reflecting disease and trauma history; counted irrespective of replacement. A shortened arch (20 teeth) can function; >8 lost usually impairs function.
4 · Bone loss / ageSteps of 0.25<0.50.5–1.0>1.0Worst posterior site: % of root length on a periapical, or mm on a bitewing (1 mm = 10%), divided by age. Age 40 with 20% → 0.5; with 50% → 1.25.
5 · Systemic / geneticPresent or notAbsent or unknown → not countedPresentDiabetes (type 1 and 2) has the strongest evidence. IL-1 genotype positive → more advanced lesions, a trend to more tooth loss, higher BOP despite SPT ("hyper-reactive"). Stress: sparse evidence.
6 · SmokingNS · FS · OS · MS · HSNon-smoker; former (quit >5 years)Occasional (<10/day); moderate (10–19/day)Heavy (≥20/day, "more than one pack")A true, dose-dependent risk factor; impairs root planing, flap and GTR outcomes; most "refractory" patients smoke; 51–56% of periodontitis in 19–30-year-olds is associated with smoking.
Overall PRA

Low = all parameters low, or at most one moderate. Moderate = at least two moderate and at most one high. High = at least two high.

BOP and residual pockets change easily with therapy; tooth loss and systemic/genetic factors can't be reversed; smoking needs great effort; BL/age falls only over several years. The diagram customises the frequency and content of SPT — no recall intervals are given.

Compare & contrast
Hirschfeld & Wasserman 1978Lang & Tonetti 2003
RoleShows why patient-level risk matters: one-sixth of patients lost most of the teethA patient-level tool to identify high-risk patients and tailor SPT
Recall4–6-monthly for everyoneFrequency and content set by risk (no intervals specified)
InflammationGingivitis often did not progress to destructionBOP is the first vector; <10% = low risk
Tooth lossThe outcome measuredOne input vector
SmokingNot assessedA key, dose-dependent vector
AgreementMaintenance is essential, and prognosis depends on the patient more than on tooth-level labels (cf. McGuire & Nunn, topic 07).
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • H&W: very long follow-up (mean 22 years), large sample (600 patients, 15,666 teeth), real-world practice, detailed tooth-type data; the pattern was the same in interim tallies at 165 and 420 patients.
  • PRA: simple and visual (useful for motivating patients); multifactorial; evidence-referenced; separates modifiable from fixed factors; guards against over- and under-treatment.
Limitations
  • H&W: retrospective, no untreated controls; one private practice; consecutive recall attenders (compliant survivors); mostly Caucasian, middle-income; periodontal cause assumed; response groups defined by the outcome (the authors call them arbitrary); treatment changed over decades; subjective "questionable" criteria; no statistical testing; examiners were the treating clinicians; tooth loss is a gross end-point; some totals don't agree (2,139 vs 2,141 questionable teeth; Table 15 totals).
  • PRA: expert-derived; cut-offs partly arbitrary (e.g. 25% BOP from one practice study); vectors unweighted; systemic factor binary and undefined; compliance and plaque not included; worst-site BL/age is crude; no recall intervals; not validated in this paper.
Clinical relevance
  • Don't extract "questionable" teeth too quickly in a compliant patient — most survived for decades with simple, thorough maintenance.
  • Identify the high-risk minority early (high BOP, many residual pockets, more bone loss than age, diabetes, heavy smoking); use the PRA to set recall frequency and content and to show patients their risk.
  • Target the modifiable vectors first: BOP and pockets (therapy, hygiene), smoking cessation, diabetes control.
Exam practice
SAQDescribe the three response groups in Hirschfeld & Wasserman and what they show.

Well-maintained (lost 0–3; 499 patients, 0.68 per patient), downhill (4–9; 76, 5.7), extreme downhill (10–23; 25, 13.3). Initial disease and treatment were similar, yet one-sixth of patients lost most of the questionable and furcated teeth → host susceptibility and case type determine tooth loss.

SAQWhich teeth were most and least likely to be lost?

Most: maxillary molars (second > first), then mandibular molars. Least: mandibular canines, then maxillary canines and mandibular first premolars. No canines were lost in the well-maintained group. Loss was bilaterally symmetrical.

SAQList the six PRA vectors with their high-risk thresholds.

BOP >25%; residual pockets ≥5 mm >8; tooth loss >8 (of 28); BL/age >1.0; a systemic/genetic factor present (e.g. diabetes, IL-1 positive); heavy smoking (≥20 a day).

SAQA 50-year-old has 30% bone loss at the worst posterior site, BOP 18%, 3 pockets ≥5 mm, 6 teeth missing, no systemic factors, and smokes 15 a day. What is their PRA?

BL/age 30/50 = 0.6 → moderate; BOP 18% → moderate; 3 pockets → low; 6 teeth lost → moderate; systemic → not counted; 15/day → moderate. Four moderate, no high → moderate risk.

SAQWhy did H&W conclude that tooth retention depends more on case type than on surgery?

A similar share (~16%) of each group had surgery during initial treatment, yet teeth lost after surgery were 14.2% (WM), 30.8% (D) and 63.3% (ED). In downhill patients surgery, splinting and hygiene only delayed loss; in well-maintained patients simple scaling sufficed.

LAQUsing Hirschfeld & Wasserman and Lang & Tonetti, discuss the importance of patient-level risk assessment in supportive periodontal therapy.
  1. The problem: periodontitis is chronic and episodic; after active therapy the patient enters SPT at a new baseline and stays at risk.
  2. H&W evidence: 600 patients, 22 years, 7.1% of teeth lost; 300 lost none; one-sixth lost most questionable and furcated teeth despite similar initial disease and treatment; canines resistant, maxillary molars vulnerable; case type outweighs surgery; inflammation doesn't always mean destruction; disease is cyclic.
  3. PRA: six vectors and thresholds, the hexagon and overall rules; modifiable vs fixed factors; customises SPT frequency and content; prevents over- and under-treatment; motivates patients.
  4. Links: McGuire & Nunn (tooth-level prognosis unreliable; smoking and diabetes matter); Samet step 3 (patient-level risk drops every tooth).
  5. Critique: H&W's retrospective selection bias, outcome-defined groups, no statistics; PRA's arbitrary thresholds, no weighting, no compliance vector, not validated.
  6. Conclusion: risk concentrates in identifiable patients — assess it at every SPT visit and tailor care.
09

Non-carious cervical lesions (NCCLs)

  • Morphology: saucer (rounded, smooth; progresses mainly in height) vs V-shaped/wedge (sharp; progresses in height and depth). Mean volume loss 0.36 mm³/year.
  • Prevalence <10% to >90%, rising with age; mostly facial, especially maxillary premolars (first premolars the most severe).
  • Multifactorial: horizontal brushing, dietary and gastric acid, medications that reduce saliva, parafunction (clenching, nail biting), possibly occlusal stress. Abfraction is controversial — FEA supports it, but there is no clinical proof, and a 2020 ORCA/IADR consensus discourages the term.
  • Grippo: NCCLs come from stress + friction + biocorrosion, shaped by modifying factors; "biocorrosion" should replace "erosion". Lingual surfaces get 5× more saliva; 47% of Senegalese patients with Hansen's disease, who couldn't brush, had NCCLs.
  • Goodacre: delay restoration; occlusal adjustment not recommended; Hawley biteplate for parafunction; for bonding to sclerotic dentine — roughen, bevel, ± retention, 30 s dentine etch, scrub adhesive (20–30 g for 20 s); SDF to arrest caries.
Paper 1 · Goodacre 2022 · narrative review + clinical guidelines

Noncarious cervical lesions: morphology and progression, prevalence, etiology, pathophysiology, and clinical guidelines for restoration

J Prosthodont 2023;32:e1–e18 (online 2022) · Loma Linda University, Indiana University–Purdue, Kerr Corporation · PubMed search

Terms

  • Tooth wear = "the cumulative loss of mineralized tooth substance due to physical or chemo-physical processes" — attrition, erosion and abrasion.
  • Attrition = tooth-to-tooth contact (gritty diet, function, parafunction). Abrasion = loss from factors other than tooth contact, e.g. vigorous horizontal brushing.
  • Erosive tooth wear = wear with erosion as the primary cause — "probably the most common reason for tooth wear" (mean prevalence 30–50% in primary and 20–45% in permanent teeth).

Morphology and progression

  • Saucer lesions: smooth, featureless surfaces with rounded borders. Wedge lesions: sharp edges, knife-edged enamel above, scratches and furrows attributed to brushing (54% of 24 extracted teeth had horizontal furrows of 5–250 µm). Also classified as shallow, concave, wedge-shaped, notched and irregular.
  • Sensitivity may be present, limited or absent; pulp vitality can be threatened in deep lesions.
  • Progression (83 lesions, 16 people, 3–5 years): mean 0.36 mm³/year (another study: 1.50 ± 0.92 mm³/year); faster as the depth-to-height ratio rises; wedges more likely to deepen. Higher risk: low salivary buffering, older age, more dietary acid.

Prevalence and location

  • Prevalence 13–63% across studies; 9.1–93% in one; 5.7–17.2% of teeth affected. A severe lesion in 29.9% at ages 26–30 vs 42.6% at 46–50. Present in the young: 29 of 40 first-year dental students (57 new lesions within 3 years).
  • Mostly facial (lingual lesions mild and uncommon). Commonest: maxillary premolars (one study: mandibular first premolars); then maxillary molars; also canines and anteriors. Most severe: first premolars. Least common: lingual of mandibular molars.

Aetiology — multifactorial

  • Brushing (excessive, horizontal); acids — carbonated drinks, citrus, wine (pH ≤3.5; cheese with wine buffers it and supplies Ca and phosphate); acidic lozenges and mouth rinses; GERD; asthma; medications that reduce saliva; abrasive foods (phytoliths). Cutting between-meal acidic snacks reduced volume loss in an RCT, yet habits rarely change even after detailed counselling.
  • Occlusal factors — conflicting: some studies link wear facets, heavy forces, premature contacts, group function, lateral excursive contacts, bruxism and lack of canine disclusion; others find no link. A systematic review: the role of occlusion is "as yet undetermined".
  • Orthodontics has no known effect on NCCLs, but uncorrected malocclusion may (e.g. over-inclined maxillary premolars in FEA); plaque around fixed appliances risks rapid caries in deep lesions. Footballers training ≤1 hour a day had more NCCLs (clenching, poorer fitness).
  • Parafunction: bruxism (dynamic) causes attrition; clenching and nail biting (static, sustained — more damaging) and TMD are significantly associated with NCCLs. Clenchers are hard to diagnose (no wear facets; tired jaws, muscle hypertrophy). Mouthguards stop attrition but not clenching loads; cloth gloves can remind nail-biters.

The abfraction debate

For
  • Tensile stress from loading flexes the tooth and concentrates at the CEJ; FEA shows overload can initiate cervical lesions, and asymmetric strains match asymmetric lesions.
  • Non-axial 200 N loads cause 10× the flexure of axial loads; the apex of a wedge is a stress riser → fatigue failure; enamel can delaminate at the DEJ under repeated oblique 100 N loads (normal function).
  • A systematic review found an association between occlusal stress and NCCLs.
  • No "smoking gun" is expected: loosened mineral is washed away by saliva and collagen fragments destroyed by enzymes, and progression is slow — so FEA modelling is the realistic test.
Against
  • No clinical study shows NCCLs caused by stress alone; the concept lacks documentation and may be flawed.
  • Loading the buccal cusps of extracted premolars produced no lesions; 299 student casts showed no link with occlusal wear.
  • "Abfraction lesion" is judged misleading; the 2020 ORCA/IADR terminology consensus discourages "abfraction" — evidence too weak for an independent cause.
  • Whatever the trigger, demineralisation occurs.

Pathophysiology — demineralisation disease

  • Demineralisation is the most prevalent chronic disease: osteoporosis (>10% worldwide), caries (untreated in 13.2% of 5–19-year-olds, 25.9% of 20–44-year-olds), and NCCLs — more prevalent than osteoporosis, so the second most common manifestation.
  • Regulated by acidity, mechanical loading and fluoride. Each NCCL is unique to its tooth; one tooth may be affected alone; bilateral symmetry is rare.
  • Cariogenic bacteria don't contribute (Fusobacteriales may even protect). Fluorapatite resists acid better than hydroxyapatite, but fluoride's effect on NCCLs is unknown.

Management

  • When to restore: there are no trials or systematic reviews. "Restorative intervention is typically best delayed as long as possible"; decide by progression and threat to vitality, function and aesthetics. Restore for reduced quality of life, sensitivity, poor aesthetics, food stagnation, or very deep lesions (strength, fracture risk; plaque in the notch → restore before caries). Extensive lesions on many teeth raise hard choices (restore vs extract and implants).
  • A prosthodontists' survey: deeper lesions (1, 2, 3 mm) and sensitive ones were more often restored; those not using mechanical retention expected shorter longevity.
  • Occlusal adjustment does not halt progression → not recommended (a study and a systematic review).
  • Hawley biteplate (anterior contact only, posteriors apart): a polysynaptic reflex weakens elevator-muscle contraction, reducing parafunctional load (full-coverage splints transmit it). Not worn 24 h (molars would over-erupt) or at meals. Based on the second author's experience.
  • Sclerotic dentine: hypermineralised, tubules blocked by crystals, little intact collagen → patchy hybrid layer, few or short resin tags, lower bond strength, slower etching.
  • Materials: no single best — composite preferred in one meta-analysis; GIC/RMGIC retained better in others (but rougher, poorer colour match); trial results conflict. The authors prefer composite.
Goodacre's restoration guidelines
  1. Isolate — rubber dam gives significantly better retention, but the clamp can cause recession. Alternative: a #000 retraction cord soaked in haemostatic agent and blotted. Keep haemostatic off dentine (it can lower bond strength; clean with air abrasion or phosphoric acid).
  2. Roughen — lightly remove surface dentine with a fine-grit diamond (gentler than a carbide bur).
  3. Mechanical retention (optional) — two ~1 mm-deep rounded depressions in the cervical floor and two in the occlusal wall (#330 or #2 round bur), ~1 mm inside the root perimeter; one per wall in small teeth.
  4. Bevel the enamel — better etching, more bonding area, gradual colour change (evidence insufficient but not negative → recommended).
  5. Adhesive — multistep or single-step, as long as total etching is included (one-step shows more marginal discolouration). Selective enamel etching before self-etch improves longevity.
  6. Etch dentine 30 s with 37% phosphoric acid: start on dentine, extend to enamel after 15 s. In very deep lesions, a light-cured Ca(OH)₂ base protects the pulp.
  7. Apply adhesive actively — light scrubbing at 20–30 g for 20 s (slight flexion of a flexible applicator, none of a stiff one); replenish self-etch adhesive.
  8. Composite — flowable ≈ sculptable clinically; flowable is easier in deep areas; large lesions → flowable layer + sculptable outer layer for wear resistance.
Caries in a cervical lesion — restore, or arrest with silver diamine fluoride

SDF is more effective than NaF; an umbrella review supports arresting and preventing root caries in older adults. Technique: dry → one drop of 38% SDF → scrub with a small applicator for 10–20 s → remove excess → keep saliva-free 3–5 min → recheck after a few days to a week and repeat if soft (a two-visit protocol also darkens caries so later restoration removes less tooth). Consent: permanent black staining (restorable later) and a temporary gingival stain — protect the gingiva with petroleum jelly or a peel-off resin glaze.

Paper 2 · Grippo 2012 · perspective

Abfraction, abrasion, biocorrosion, and the enigma of noncarious cervical lesions: a 20-year perspective

J Esthet Restor Dent 2012;24(1):10–23 (online 2011) · Grippo coined "abfraction" in 1991 (amended 2004)

Three arguments

  1. "Biocorrosion" should supplant "erosion". It covers chemical, biochemical and electrochemical degradation — endogenous and exogenous acids, proteolytic enzymes and piezoelectric effects (dentine only). "Erosion" is a physical mechanism: wear by the flow of liquids.
  2. "Abfraction" (microfracture from stress concentration) has become a "buzzword" implying one cause — it should not be used for all NCCLs.
  3. Each lesion reflects the interplay of stress, friction and biocorrosion, unique to the case, plus modifying factors.

Mechanisms

  • Stress: compression, tension, flexion, shear; effect depends on magnitude, direction, frequency, site and duration, and on tooth form and stability. Fatigue damage at the cervix is distant from the contact. Stress acts synergistically with corrodents and abrasives — biocorrosion is accelerated under stress (thermodynamics).
  • Combined mechanisms: static stress-biocorrosion (corrodent + sustained load: clenching, swallowing, active orthodontics); cyclic/fatigue stress-biocorrosion (corrodent + intermittent load: bruxing, tapping, chewing); abrasion/biocorrosion (brushing straight after an acidic drink or regurgitation).
  • Tribology: wear may be abrasive, adhesive, fatigue, fretting, erosive (liquid flow) or corrosive (dissolution); friction generates heat that the lubricant (saliva) must remove.
  • Tissues: enamel is 85% inorganic (acid-soluble); dentine is 33% organic (proteolysis). Demineralised dentine matrix normally limits further loss, but pepsin and trypsin degrade it (together more than either) — they reach the mouth in GERD, regurgitation and bulimia; hiatal hernia (common over 50) → more biocorrosion expected as the population ages. Caries itself is microbial biocorrosion.
  • Piezoelectric effects occur in dentine, not enamel, and can move calcium ions — needs verification.
  • Stress-biocorrosion appears as NCCLs on plaque-free cervical surfaces; with poor hygiene the same sites develop root caries.

Evidence

  • Photoelastic and FEA studies: the cervical region is the zone of maximum stress. Grippo & Masi: strain-gauge flexion; static load in acid accelerated enamel loss.
  • In vitro: Palamara 2001 (cyclic load + 1% lactic acid → cervical enamel effects); Staninec 2005 and Mishra 2006 (dentine beams: load + low pH → more loss at the fixed end, the "cervix"); Noma 2007 (cementum fatigue cracks from the cervix).
  • Clinical: cervical restorations dislodge under loading; gold foils changed shape without canine guidance but not with canine rise (Fig 4).
  • Faye 2006 (Senegal): 48 of 102 (47%) non-brushing patients with Hansen's disease had NCCLs → occlusal stress + acidic drinks (bissap), without toothbrush abrasion (Fig 3).
  • Loading facts: ~1 million tooth contacts a year; ~1,500 swallows a day; the jaw is closed 683 ms per swallow vs 194 ms per chewing contact; swallowing force 66.5 lb (296 N) > chewing 58.7 lb (261 N).

Modifying factors (Table 2)

FactorEffect
SalivaBuffering, composition, flow, pH, viscosity. 5× more saliva lingually (serous, bicarbonate-buffered) → few lingual NCCLs; facial surfaces have mucous saliva with little buffering. Xerostomia; mouth breathing dries the anterior labial area.
TeethComposition, form, structure. Mobility is negatively correlated with NCCLs — a mobile tooth tilts and the PDL absorbs stress; a stable tooth flexes at the cervix. Arch form resists lingual flexure but allows facial flexure.
Positional prominenceFacially prominent teeth → brushing abrasion; occlusally prominent teeth invite eccentric parafunctional contacts (wear facets are clues); recessed teeth are shielded.
Occlusal formSteep, non-axial premature contacts raise cervical stress; flat-worn teeth load axially — why NCCLs are rare in "primitive" groups.
Tongue, diet, habits, healthThe tongue cleans lingual surfaces; acid frequency; noxious habits; medical history.
  • A lesion forms when the pathodynamic factors exceed the tooth's "odontolytic threshold".
  • Brushing as a stress raiser (Davis) fits the facial distribution but not isolated lesions beside unscathed teeth, or lesions under crown margins and gingiva.
  • Clinical message: before naming one mechanism, take a full medical and dental history, examine the occlusion, inventory the diet, review hygiene, assess saliva and note positional prominence — then treat the causes using the schema.
Compare & contrast
Goodacre 2022Grippo 2012
AbfractionPresents both sides; notes the 2020 consensus discourages the termA real cofactor (not the sole cause); the author coined it
TerminologyAttrition, abrasion, erosive tooth wearStress, friction, biocorrosion (erosion = liquid flow only)
OcclusionRole undetermined; occlusal adjustment not recommended; Hawley biteplatePremature contacts and lack of canine guidance matter
DistributionEach lesion unique; bilateral symmetry rareExplained by positional prominence, mobility, saliva
ScopeMorphology, prevalence, aetiology, pathophysiology, restoration protocol, SDFMechanisms and terminology; diagnosis of causes, no restorative protocol
AgreementMultifactorial; facial premolars most affected; saliva, diet and parafunction matter; history and prevention first.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Goodacre: comprehensive and recent; balanced on the controversy; step-by-step protocols (restoration, SDF); quantitative progression and prevalence data.
  • Grippo: a clear framework (schema + modifying factors) that looks beyond brushing; brings in engineering (tribology, fatigue); explains clinical oddities (lingual sparing, isolated lesions).
Limitations
  • Goodacre: narrative (no systematic search); many recommendations rest on lab data or the authors' experience (retention, 30 s etch, Hawley); third author employed by Kerr (no conflicts declared).
  • Grippo: written by the term's originator; evidence mainly in vitro (beams, FEA, strain gauges), cases and personal communications; no systematic search; the 2020 terminology consensus quoted by Goodacre uses "erosive tooth wear" rather than "biocorrosion".
  • Both: no clinical trials of causation; prevalence varies hugely between studies.
Clinical relevance
  • Treat the NCCL as a symptom: diet history (acid frequency, rinses, reflux), brushing technique, parafunction (clenching, nail biting), occlusion and saliva.
  • Prevent and monitor; restore for sensitivity, aesthetics, food stagnation, depth or caries.
  • When bonding: roughen sclerotic dentine, bevel enamel, etch dentine 30 s, scrub the adhesive, consider retention depressions; flowable then sculptable composite. Don't adjust the occlusion to stop progression.
Exam practice
SAQDefine attrition, abrasion, erosive tooth wear, abfraction and biocorrosion.

Attrition: tooth-to-tooth wear. Abrasion: wear by factors other than tooth contact (e.g. horizontal brushing). Erosive tooth wear: wear with erosion (acid) as the primary cause. Abfraction: microfracture and loss of tooth substance in areas of stress concentration (Grippo). Biocorrosion: chemical, biochemical or electrochemical degradation — acids, proteolytic enzymes, piezoelectric effects; Grippo would restrict "erosion" to physical wear by liquid flow.

SAQCompare saucer-shaped and wedge-shaped NCCLs.

Saucer: rounded, smooth, featureless, rounded borders; progresses mainly in height. Wedge: V-shaped, sharp edges, knife-edged enamel, brushing scratches and furrows; progresses in height and depth (faster as depth/height rises); its apex is a stress riser in FEA.

SAQWhy is abfraction controversial, and why is it hard to prove?

FEA shows cervical stress and fatigue under non-axial loads and a review found an association — but no clinical study shows stress alone causes NCCLs, loading extracted teeth produced no lesions, casts showed no link with wear, and the 2020 consensus discourages the term. It's hard to prove because there is no "smoking gun": loosened mineral and collagen are removed by saliva and enzymes, and progression is slow.

SAQWhy are NCCLs uncommon on lingual surfaces, according to Grippo?

Lingual surfaces receive about 5× more serous, bicarbonate-buffered saliva than the vestibule, and the tongue cleans them; they are also brushed less. The arch form resists lingual flexure but allows facial flexure, concentrating stress facially.

SAQHow does sclerotic dentine affect bonding, and how does Goodacre modify the technique?

Tubules are blocked by crystals and intact collagen is lacking → patchy hybrid layer, short resin tags, lower bond strength, slower etching. Modifications: roughen with a fine diamond; bevel and etch the enamel; etch dentine 30 s with 37% phosphoric acid; scrub the adhesive (20–30 g for 20 s); ± ~1 mm retention depressions.

SAQDescribe the SDF protocol for caries in a cervical lesion.

Consent (permanent black lesion; temporary gingival stain) and protect the gingiva; dry; one drop of 38% SDF scrubbed in for 10–20 s; remove excess; keep saliva-free 3–5 min; review after a few days to a week and repeat if soft; restore tooth-coloured later if wanted.

LAQDiscuss the aetiology of non-carious cervical lesions and outline their management, contrasting the views of Grippo and Goodacre.
  1. Presentation: saucer vs wedge; progression 0.36 mm³/year; prevalence <10–90%, rising with age; facial maxillary premolars.
  2. Aetiology: multifactorial — friction (horizontal brushing), chemical (dietary and gastric acid; pepsin and trypsin), stress (parafunction, occlusion, swallowing), modified by saliva, position, mobility, arch form, diet and health. Grippo's schema and odontolytic threshold vs Goodacre's demineralisation-disease view.
  3. Abfraction debate: FEA and in-vitro support; no smoking gun; no clinical proof; 2020 consensus; biocorrosion vs erosive tooth wear.
  4. Management: history, diet and saliva, habits, occlusion; prevention; monitor; Hawley biteplate; no occlusal adjustment; restore when indicated with the bonding protocol; SDF for caries.
  5. Appraisal: both narrative; Grippo's stake in the term and in-vitro evidence; Goodacre's opinion-based protocol and industry affiliation. Conclude: identify each patient's dominant factors.
10

Dentine hypersensitivity (DH)

  • DH = pain arising from exposed dentine, typically to thermal, chemical, tactile or osmotic stimuli. It needs exposed dentine ("lesion localisation") and patent tubules ("lesion initiation").
  • Hydrodynamic theory (Brännström) is the most accepted → treat by occluding tubules or desensitising the nerve (K⁺).
  • Prevalence 4–74% (usually 10–30%); most sufferers aged 20–40, peaking at the end of the third decade; upper premolars most affected; highest in periodontal patients.
  • West (systematic review, 105 RCTs, 11 agents, no meta-analysis): recommended toothpastes — arginine (high-quality evidence), stannous fluoride (high), strontium acetate (moderate), CSPS (low). Potassium: not recommended. No professional agent can be ranked above another; fluoride varnishes showed limited or no efficacy.
  • Bartold (narrative, 2006): KNO₃, SnF₂, NaF, MFP and strontium chloride toothpastes are safe and beneficial; 5% KNO₃ + fluoride has US FDA Category 1 status. Only 24 of 105 trials in West were free of industry support.
Paper 1 · Bartold 2006 · narrative review

Dentinal hypersensitivity: a review

Aust Dent J 2006;51(3):212–218 · University of Adelaide, Colgate Australian Clinical Dental Research Centre

How dentine becomes exposed and sensitive

  • Definition (Addy): pain arising from exposed dentine, typically in response to thermal, chemical, tactile or osmotic stimuli. Also called cervical dentinal sensitivity.
  • Enamel or cementum is lost through attrition, abrasion or erosion, or enamel and cementum fail to meet at the CEJ (developmental). Usually several factors combine.
  • The common feature is open tubules linking the mouth to the pulp; without them, DH is unlikely. Established sensitivity can persist even after tubules are occluded by smear layer or pellicle — the pulp may become irreversibly sensitive.
  • Treatment aims: restore impermeability (partly or totally occlude the tubules) and/or damp the pulpal nerves.

Three theories

TheoryIdeaStatus
Odontoblastic transductionOdontoblast processes exposed at the surface are excited and release neurotransmitters onto nerve endingsNo neurotransmitters have been found to be produced or released by odontoblast processes
NeuralStimuli act directly on nerve endings within the tubulesSome support (unmyelinated fibres in outer root dentine) but still theoretical
Hydrodynamic (Brännström)Temperature, physical or osmotic changes disturb the fluid in tubules open at the surface and the pulp → a receptor (a "baroreceptor") triggers neural dischargeBy far the most widely accepted

Air drying draws fluid outwards; heat and cold expand or contract it; sugar, acid and salt move it osmotically. Tactile pain is harder to explain, though abrasion of the surface may move fluid.

Epidemiology and presentation

  • Prevalence 4–74% across 19 studies (Table 1), usually 10–30%. Many more people report sensitive teeth than meet clinical criteria. Examples: 73% of UK periodontal referrals, 67.6% in a Hong Kong hospital clinic, ~4% in UK general practice.
  • Most sufferers are 20–40, peaking at the end of the third decade and falling in the fourth and fifth (sclerosis, secondary dentine, long-term fluoride use) — despite more recession and wear with age.
  • Upper premolars > upper first molars; incisors least. Slightly more in females (not significant). Highest in periodontal patients, recession, and smokers with periodontitis.
  • Not serious, but unpleasant and can dictate diet; described as dull or sharp, vague or specific, intermittent or constant. Usually managed at home with over-the-counter products.
  • Differential diagnosis: carious dentine, inflamed pulps and cracked cusps can mimic DH.
  • Plaque: good plaque control is linked to less DH, but its role is controversial — many patients with recession and little plaque are still sensitive.
  • Ideal agent (Dababneh): non-irritant to the pulp, relatively painless, easy to apply, rapid, permanently effective, no staining. Responses are subjective, and "all currently available treatments appear to work".

Treatment strategies (Table 2)

StrategyAgentsBartold's comments
Nerve desensitisationPotassium nitrateHodosh's early claim was poorly controlled; Tarbet: 5% KNO₃ in a low-abrasive paste worked for up to 4 weeks vs control; 5% and 10% gels also effective; no pulpal changes. Cochrane (Poulsen 2001): no strong evidence, though significant differences favoured KNO₃. Mechanism probably K⁺ depolarising sensory nerves (unconfirmed in intact teeth); little effect on fluid flow.
Anti-inflammatoryCorticosteroidsNot particularly useful in trials
Plug / sclerose tubulesCa(OH)₂, potassium oxalate, NaF, SnF₂, sodium MFP, strontium chloride; fluoride iontophoresis; burnishingCa(OH)₂: immediate but short-lived; irritates gingiva. NaF: acid resistance + precipitates in tubules. MFP: effective, but no visible change on SEM. SnF₂: a calcific barrier or surface precipitate. Iontophoresis: immediate relief, symptoms return over ~6 months.
Protein precipitants (formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, silver nitrate); casein phosphopeptidesAldehydes: little or no effect in some formulations; strong fixatives — keep off the gingiva. CPP: no published efficacy studies.
Seal the dentineGIC, composite, resins, varnishes, sealantsGood until the adhesive breaks away → for localised DH
Cover or restoreGrafts (lateral sliding, free gingival, connective tissue, coronally repositioned flaps); crowns or restorationsGrafting is not very predictable for sensitivity; restorations are invasive → significant cervical loss or a last resort
LasersNd:YAG (+ NaF varnish: up to 90% of tubules occluded); CO₂ (+ SnF₂ gel: occlusion up to 6 months)Largely experimental
  • Combination products: early KNO₃ pastes lacked fluoride, so patients needed two pastes; in 1992 the US FDA gave Category 1 (safe and effective) status to 5% KNO₃ + fluoride toothpastes.
  • Safety: extensive toxicity testing and regulatory review; a Medline search to December 2005 found no adverse-reaction reports for strontium chloride or KNO₃ and only a few for fluoride (mostly children). DH is a localised condition, so treating it can't mask systemic disease.
  • Simple daily plaque removal is one of the most effective treatments — over time salivary minerals occlude the tubules (the paper writes "demineralization").
  • Conclusion: DH can be managed with many in-office and home approaches; some work better than others. KNO₃, SnF₂, NaF, MFP and strontium chloride have been studied extensively for home use and are safe and beneficial.
Paper 2 · West, Seong & Davies 2015 · systematic review of RCTs

Management of dentine hypersensitivity: efficacy of professionally and self-administered agents

J Clin Periodontol 2015;42(Suppl 16):S256–S302 · Bristol Dental School · no funding; no conflicts declared

Context and mechanisms

  • No gold-standard treatment exists. DH is a common, transient pain — immediate on stimulating exposed dentine, resolving when the stimulus is removed (Holland 1997); short, sharp and arresting. It affects quality of life: 28% of 3,000 people said it mattered importantly to them; 42% of 18–35-year-olds report sensitivity.
  • Risk factors: recession (toothbrushing, periodontal disease); a "healthy" erosive diet and lifestyle (tooth wear, especially young adults); more teeth retained into old age.
  • Pain needs lesion localisation (exposed dentine) and lesion initiation (patent tubules) (Addy 2002) — hence tubule occlusion is the favoured approach, its success depending on resisting daily acid challenges. Alternatively, potassium ions diffuse along the tubules and block intradental nerves.
  • Change the causes first. Most treatment is a self-applied toothpaste; professional agents for severe or non-responding cases.

Methods

  • Question: how effective are self-applied and professionally applied agents for DH pain vs placebo/benchmark and/or other actives? PRISMA.
  • Search: PubMed, Medline, Cochrane trials register + hand search; English only; 14–21 July 2014.
  • Included: human RCTs (parallel or split-mouth) vs a negative control (placebo, or a conventional fluoride benchmark) or a positive comparator. Excluded: reviews, case reports, abstracts, in-vitro and in-situ studies.
  • Outcome: pain to tactile, evaporative (air blast) or thermal stimuli. Short-term = immediate to 1 week; long-term = ≥2 weeks.
  • Quality: two screeners; risk of bias (design, intervention, outcomes, statistics → low/moderate/high); body of evidence graded high → very low on bias, directness, consistency, precision and publication bias.
  • Result: 105 RCTs, 11 agents; too heterogeneous for meta-analysis → narrative synthesis.

Verdict by agent

AgentPapersKey findingsEvidenceVerdict
Arginine (+ calcium carbonate)30Toothpaste consistently beat fluoride controls and always beat potassium; vs strontium acetate 3 similar, 3 arginine better; inferior to SnF₂ (2 studies). Rinse and prophylaxis paste favourable but low-quality evidence.High vs F/K · Mod vs SrRecommend (toothpaste)
Stannous fluoride17Better than negative controls; better than arginine; SnF₂/K pastes better than K or negative controlsHigh vs arginine · Mod vs FRecommend
Strontium18Acetate (2010–13): better than a negative control in 2 of 3 studies; similar to, or slightly less than, arginine. Chloride (mostly ≤2008): not consistently better than controls.Mod acetate · Low chlorideRecommend acetate
CSPS (calcium sodium phosphosilicate, NovaMin)12Consistently better than negative, fluoride and potassium; better than SnF₂ gel in one study; 5 toothpaste trials at high risk of biasLowRecommend (toothpaste, with caution)
Potassium (nitrate, citrate, chloride…)25Inferior to arginine, CSPS and SnF₂ (and to resin and sealant); often no better than a negative control; needs ~2 weeks; a poor positive controlHigh that it is inferiorCannot recommend
PVM/MA polymers6Combined with arginine, triclosan or potassiumLowCannot recommend
Casein derivatives (ACP, CPP-ACP)3All professionally applied; ACP no better than water in one trialVery lowCannot recommend
Oxalates9Mostly professional; equivocal vs water; inconsistent vs resinsLowLimited evidence
Resins (Gluma, Seal & Protect, GIC)9Consistently reduce DH; Gluma inferior to other bonding agents and GICLowEffective — can't rank
Varnishes7Reduce DH except fluoride varnishes (limited or no effect); work only while on the toothLowCan't rank
Lasers (Nd:YAG, GaAlAs, laser toothbrush)8Reduce pain but minimal advantage over comparators; strong placebo effect in other reviewsLowCan't rank

Discussion

  • Pain is subjective. Grossman's principles (1935): easy to administer, effective, safe, fast-acting, long-lasting. Trials have moved from 2–8-week (up to 6–12-month) designs to immediate-relief studies.
  • Holland 1997: use ≥2 clinically relevant stimuli and both negative and positive controls — many trials had only one control.
  • Heterogeneity: many actives, salts and formulations (even silica abrasives occlude tubules). Parallel designs avoid carry-over; split-mouth suits varnish or laser, not toothpaste.
  • Industry: only 24 of 105 studies had no industry sponsorship or donation; most followed GCP with moderate risk of bias; publication bias couldn't be assessed.
West's conclusions

Arginine, stannous fluoride, CSPS and strontium toothpastes are effective — with twice-daily use they should bring rapid, considerable relief, and they are cheap and available over the counter. Self-applied desensitising toothpaste is the first choice, then professional agents, none of which can be recommended over another. Aetiological factors must be part of management.

Compare & contrast — the key exam point
IssueBartold 2006West 2015
DesignNarrative review: no search strategy or appraisal; Colgate-affiliated centreSystematic review: explicit search, criteria, risk of bias, evidence grading (no meta-analysis)
Potassium5% KNO₃ effective (Tarbet), FDA Category 1, safe and beneficial — while noting the weak Cochrane evidenceHigh-quality evidence it is inferior to arginine, CSPS and SnF₂ → cannot recommend; a poor positive control
StrontiumStrontium chloride safe and beneficialChloride low-quality; acetate recommended
Newer agentsNo arginine or CSPS trials yet; casein unstudied; lasers experimentalArginine and CSPS recommended; casein very low; lasers weak (placebo effect)
FluorideNaF solutions and iontophoresis effectiveFluoride varnish limited or no efficacy
AgreementHydrodynamic mechanism → occlusion or nerve desensitisation; home toothpaste first; sealants, restorations and grafts for localised or refractory cases; tackle the cause.
Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Bartold: a clear overview of theory, epidemiology and the whole range of treatments; considers safety.
  • West: systematic and transparent; RCTs only; risk of bias and evidence grading; clear agent-by-agent recommendations; separates self-applied and professional agents; reports industry involvement.
Limitations
  • Bartold: no systematic search or appraisal; Colgate-affiliated; predates arginine and CSPS toothpastes; relies on older, poorly controlled trials.
  • West: no meta-analysis; English only; in-situ evidence excluded; 81 of 105 trials industry-linked; includes trials by the first author; subjective pain outcomes and varied follow-up.
Clinical relevance
  • Diagnose first: exclude caries, cracked cusps and pulpitis; then find the cause of exposure (erosion, brushing abrasion, recession, periodontal treatment).
  • Manage: remove causes → twice-daily desensitising toothpaste (SnF₂, arginine, CSPS or strontium acetate) → review → professional agents for localised or refractory sites → restoration or grafting as a last resort.
Exam practice
SAQDefine dentine hypersensitivity and explain the hydrodynamic theory.

Pain arising from exposed dentine in response to thermal, chemical, tactile or osmotic stimuli (Addy, cited by Bartold) — short and sharp, resolving when the stimulus is removed (Holland, cited by West). Hydrodynamic theory (Brännström): stimuli move the fluid in tubules open at the surface and the pulp, triggering nerve receptors at the pulp–dentine border → pain. Air drying draws fluid outward; cold contracts it; sugar and acid act osmotically.

SAQDescribe the epidemiology of DH (Bartold).

Prevalence 4–74% (usually 10–30%); self-report exceeds clinical diagnosis. Most sufferers 20–40, peaking at the end of the third decade, then falling (sclerosis, secondary dentine, fluoride). Upper premolars most affected, incisors least; slight female excess; highest in periodontal patients, recession and smokers with periodontitis.

SAQWhat are the two main ways desensitising agents work? Give examples.

(1) Tubule occlusion — SnF₂, arginine–calcium carbonate, CSPS, strontium, oxalates, resins, varnishes; success depends on resisting acid challenge. (2) Nerve desensitisation — potassium salts (K⁺ diffuses down the tubules and blocks intradental nerves).

SAQWhich toothpastes did West recommend, and why not potassium?

Arginine (high-quality evidence), stannous fluoride (high), strontium acetate (moderate) and CSPS (low, but consistently favourable). Potassium: high-quality evidence that it is inferior to arginine, CSPS and SnF₂; often no better than a negative control; slow (~2 weeks).

SAQGive three methodological problems in DH trials identified by West.

Subjective pain outcomes and varied stimuli (Holland: ≥2 stimuli); missing negative or positive controls (potassium a poor positive control); heterogeneous actives and formulations; split-mouth designs unsuitable for toothpaste; industry involvement (only 24 of 105 independent); unknown publication bias.

LAQDiscuss the aetiology, diagnosis and management of dentine hypersensitivity, contrasting Bartold 2006 and West 2015.
  1. Definition and mechanism: exposure (attrition, abrasion, erosion, recession, CEJ gap) + patent tubules; three theories, hydrodynamic most accepted.
  2. Epidemiology and risk: usually 10–30%; peak around 30; upper premolars; periodontal patients; erosive diets in young adults; quality-of-life impact.
  3. Diagnosis: exclude caries, cracks, pulpitis; identify causes.
  4. Management: remove cause → home toothpaste → professional agents → invasive options. Bartold's strategies (KNO₃ with FDA Category 1, fluorides, strontium chloride, sealants, grafts, lasers) vs West's evidence (arginine, SnF₂, Sr acetate, CSPS recommended; potassium not; professional agents unrankable; fluoride varnish weak).
  5. Appraisal: narrative vs systematic; industry links in both; evolving products; heterogeneous trials.
  6. Conclusion: an evidence-based occluding toothpaste first, plus control of the cause.
11

Tooth wear — assessment, prevention & when to restore

  • Physiological wear (both papers cite Lambrechts 1989): vertical enamel loss ~20–38 µm/year (Mehta); occlusal enamel ~15 µm/year on premolars and ~29 µm/year on molars (Loomans). Severe wear rises from 3% at age 20 to 17% (Mehta) or 15% (Loomans) at 70 — both cite Van't Spijker.
  • Loomans separates severe wear (an amount: dentine exposed and ≥⅓ of the clinical crown lost) from pathological wear (atypical for age and causing pain or discomfort, functional or aesthetic problems).
  • Mehta: history → examination → special tests → diagnosis (type, severity, location; TWI, BEWE, ACE; Turner & Missirlian) → five-phase plan → seven preventive measures → monitoring. Most cases can be managed passively.
  • Loomans: prevention, counselling and monitoring whatever the severity; restore only when the wear concerns the patient or clinician, never with definitive restorations during active disease; use additive, minimally invasive techniques (Dahl, DSO, mould and stamp, minimally invasive indirect) and avoid the restorative death spiral.
  • "Once a restorative patient, always a restorative patient." Keep careful records — conservative care can attract accusations of supervised neglect.
Paper 1 · Mehta 2012 · narrative clinical guide (verifiable CPD)

Current concepts on the management of tooth wear: part 1. Assessment, treatment planning and strategies for the prevention and the passive management of tooth wear

Br Dent J 2012;212(1):17–27 · Mehta, Banerji, Millar (King's College London) & Suarez-Feito (University of Oviedo) · part 1 of a four-part series

Definitions

  • Tooth wear (TW): surface loss of dental hard tissue from causes other than caries, trauma or developmental disorders. A normal physiological process that is macroscopically irreversible and cumulative with age.
  • Multifactorial — erosion, abrasion, abfraction and attrition — and a single cause is hard (at times impossible) to isolate. Tooth surface loss (TSL) (Eccles 1982) covers all causes, identified or not, including trauma, developmental conditions (amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta) and iatrogenic wear.
  • Pathological TW: wear causing functional or aesthetic concern, disproportionate for the patient's age, causing discomfort, or progressing at a rate of grave concern to the patient or operator.

Scale of the problem

  • Adults: severe wear rises from 3% at 20 to 17% at 70 (Van't Spijker, systematic review of 186 prevalence studies). In a German study (Bernhardt 2004) mean wear scores (0–3) rose from 0.6 at 20–29 years to 1.4 at 70–79.
  • Children: erosion entered the UK Children's Dental Health Survey in 1993 — palatal erosion of the maxillary incisors in 25% of 11-year-olds and 32% of 14-year-olds (some into dentine or pulp); almost half of 5–6-year-olds had erosion of primary teeth, almost 25% with dentine or pulp involvement. The 1996/97 reassessment found a trend towards more erosion at 3.5–4.5 years, particularly in children drinking carbonated drinks almost daily.
  • Dugmore & Rock 2004: 1,753 children examined at 12 and followed for 2 years — 59.7% had wear at baseline; dentine exposure rose from 2.7% to 8.9%.
  • UK soft-drink consumption rose 7-fold from the 1950s to the 1990s; children and adolescents make 65% of purchases (a reported per-capita intake of 15 L). More patients present with wear because of changing diets and lifestyles (especially the young) and because older people keep their teeth longer.
  • Erosion sources: extrinsic (diet; acids in the workplace) or intrinsic — regurgitation, involuntary (e.g. hiatus hernia) or voluntary (eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia nervosa).
  • What makes management hard: reaching an accurate diagnosis; knowing when to move from passive management to restoration; knowing how to restore a severely worn dentition to a stable result; unfamiliarity with contemporary materials and techniques.
Table 1 · pH of commonly consumed UK drinks (Kelleher & Bishop)
ManufacturerBrandpH
Pepsi-ColaDiet2.95
Coca-ColaRegular3.15
Coca-ColaCaffeine-free diet3.30
LucozadeSport Orange3.78
TangoDiet Orange2.80
Orange juice3.50

History

Holbrook & Arnadottir: to prevent or reduce wear, recognise the problem, grade its severity, diagnose the likely cause(s) and monitor progress to judge prevention. Finding the cause may take several visits, as patients can be reluctant to disclose sensitive information. Chief complaints: aesthetics (fractured or unattractive teeth or restorations, discolouration), function (chewing efficiency; lip, cheek or tongue biting) and, less often, comfort (pain, sensitivity).

HistoryWhat to look for
MedicalAsthma inhalers (steroid) and effervescent medicines — asthma drugs range from pH 4.31 (Bricanyl powder) to pH 9.30 (Ventolin aerosol); aspirin, chewable vitamin C, iron preparations; drugs causing xerostomia (diuretics, antidepressants). Reflux — anorexia or bulimia nervosa (female:male 10:1.5), hiatus hernia, sphincter incompetence, oesophagitis, raised gastric pressure; cyclical vomiting syndrome; rumination; pregnancy (abdominal pressure, morning sickness). Heartburn is key, but patients with subclinical reflux may be unaware; reflux may be associated with oesophageal carcinoma. Some cases need referral to the GMP.
DentalPast care; toothbrush type and the intensity, frequency and timing of brushing; toothpaste abrasivity; motivation, negative attitudes or phobia (may not suit complex care at first); experience with removable prostheses.
Social & dietStress and occupation (also affects attendance); smoking; alcohol (binge drinking is often followed by vomiting); diet — citrus, pickles, vinegar, coarse food, cola, fruit juices, carbonated drinks: frequency, quantity, duration and method of consumption; a 3-day consecutive diet diary (Watson & Burke). Habits — pipe smoking, pen or pencil biting, holding objects between the teeth. LSD and ecstasy; frequent swimmers (chlorinated pools); copper-mine workers (sulphuric acid → labial erosion of the maxillary anteriors).

Examination

  • Extra-oral: TMJs and muscles (bilateral palpation; tenderness, clicking, crepitus, deviation, pain); maximum opening (<40 mm between incisal edges = restricted); parotid enlargement (often in bulimia); facial proportions — freeway space from the resting and occlusal vertical dimensions (callipers or a Willis gauge; also phonetics, especially sibilants, soft-tissue contours, jaw tracking, electrical muscle stimulation); smile line, lip line and midline.
  • Intra-oral: soft tissues (buccal keratoses, scalloped tongue, signs of xerostomia). Saliva protects enamel by supplying the acquired pellicle and by buffering, which promotes remineralisation. Oral hygiene and BPE (± a full 6-point chart); dental chart (caries, restorations and failures, fractures, abrasion and erosion lesions). Record the location (localised, anterior/posterior, generalised) and severity (enamel only, into dentine, severe).
  • Occlusion: crowding, rotation, tilting, drifting, spacing, over-eruption, mobility; overbite and overjet; a stable CO and the ICP contacts; how easily the mandible is guided into the retruded arc (deprogrammers — cotton rolls, wooden spatulas, a Lucia jig or a full-coverage stabilisation splint); the RCP and any CR→CO slide, its direction and whether it is mainly vertical or horizontal (it may provide space for restorative material); canine guidance or group function, protrusion, working and non-working interferences; denture-bearing areas and prosthesis fit if partially dentate.

Special tests

  • Long-cone periapicals of worn teeth and any teeth to be restored: bone loss, root form, pulp chambers, existing root fillings, caries, lamina dura, retained roots, periapical pathology. Teeth with poor root form or bone support, unfavourable crown:root ratios, pathology or a guarded endodontic prognosis are poor teeth for complex restorations — especially if the crown:root ratio will increase.
  • Articulated study casts (vacuum-mixed die stone) on at least a semi-adjustable articulator in CR: occlusion without soft-tissue or muscle interference, over-eruption, contacts in CR and excursions, interferences, space gained in CR, the effect of "opening the bite", trial adjustments, and the vertical and horizontal components of the CR→CO slide.
  • Sensibility tests on every affected tooth — loss of vitality is common in severe wear (ethyl chloride, warm gutta-percha, electric; true vitality only with Doppler flow).
  • Photographs (anterior, left and right posterior, occlusal of both arches) and salivary analysis (stimulated and unstimulated flow, buffering).
  • Diagnostic wax-up / mock-up: a visual and communication aid for aesthetics, shape, length and inclination. Duplicated in stone, it gives a vacuum-formed PVC matrix to try the changes in the mouth with provisional crown and bridge material, plus tooth-reduction guides, provisionals and PVS indices for direct composite.

Diagnosis — four types of lesion

Describe the type(s) of lesion, their extent and location, and their severity.

TypeDefinitionAppearance and sites
AttritionWear from tooth-to-tooth contact, as in chewing, possibly with an abrasive substance (Eccles)Incisal and occlusal contacts: first a small polished facet on a cusp or ridge, or a flattened incisal edge → lower cusps, flatter inclines, dentine exposure → marked shortening of the clinical crown
ErosionChemical loss of tooth surface not involving bacteria; intrinsic or extrinsic acidBilateral concave defects without the chalkiness or roughness of caries. Early: shallow, smooth, glazed, no developmental ridges or stain lines, plaque-free. Later: dull exposed dentine, "cupping" of posterior occlusal surfaces and incisal edges. Extrinsic → labial maxillary anteriors (scooped-out depressions); intrinsic → palatal maxillary anteriors (whole palatal surface concave). Perimolysis: the classic palatal lesions of chronic vomiting.
AbrasionAbnormal mechanical wear by a foreign object or substance, independent of occlusion (Shafer)Pattern set by the object. Overzealous brushing → rounded or V-shaped ditches at the buccal CEJ, mostly canines and premolars. Notched upper central incisal edges from tacks, nails, pins, thread, pipe stems, hairpins or wind instruments.
AbfractionLoss from eccentric occlusal loads → compressive and tensile stress at the cervical fulcrum (Imfeld)Tensile stress weakens cervical hydroxyapatite → wedge-shaped defects with sharp rims at the CEJ. Less common on mobile teeth; often marked by repeatedly failing cervical restorations ("cervical stress lesions"). Extent depends on the size, duration, direction, frequency and location of the forces.

Hattab: erosion seems to be the most common cause of tooth surface loss, and regurgitation erosion the most damaging — though patterns vary between cultures. Cervical lesions can become caries-prone in vulnerable patients.

Severity and indices

  • Physiological (normal for age) → prevention and monitoring only. Pathological (excessive for age) → may also need active restoration. But normal levels of wear for each age group are not yet defined, and it is unknown whether wear is episodic or progressive throughout life. Distinguish inherited conditions (amelogenesis or dentinogenesis imperfecta).
  • Tooth Wear Index (Smith & Knight, Table 2): the most popular index; compares individuals and monitors progression; criticised because it does not relate aetiology to outcome.
  • BEWE (Basic Erosive Wear Examination; Bartlett 2010, with European colleagues), based on the BPE: designed to be simple to use and easy to record, and to show that wear was examined. Each sextant is scored by its worst tooth: 0 no wear; 1 initial loss of surface texture; 2 <50% loss of surface; 3 >50% loss. The aggregate score guides management, but its sensitivity and specificity still need study.
  • ACE (anterior clinical erosive classification; Vailati & Belser, Table 3): for the upper anteriors — grades severity and suggests treatment, using palatal dentine exposure, incisal edges, remaining crown length, labial enamel and pulp vitality. The "sandwich approach" = a resin-based material for the palatal wear, then a labial ceramic veneer.

4Buccal, lingual and occlusal complete loss of enamel, pulp exposure or exposure of secondary dentine · incisal pulp exposure or exposure of secondary dentine

Location

  • Classify wear as localised (say where: anterior, posterior, maxillary, mandibular) or generalised.
  • Mandibular anteriors erode less than maxillary ones: the tongue holds intrinsic acid against the upper palatal surfaces, while the lower teeth are bathed in submandibular and sublingual saliva; posterior teeth are protected by parotid saliva. The commonest sites in prevalence studies are molar occlusal surfaces and incisal edges.
  • Localised wear: is there space for restorative material in ICP (CO) or CR? Which teeth guide lateral and protrusive movements?
  • Generalised wear: gauge how much dento-alveolar compensation has occurred (the freeway space may or may not have increased), then assign a Turner & Missirlian category after assessing the OVD:
    1. Excessive wear with loss of OVD
    2. Excessive wear without loss of OVD, but with space available
    3. Excessive wear without loss of OVD, but with limited space
    Slow wear with secondary supra-eruption of the dento-alveolar processes is thought to explain categories 2 and 3. The category has a "paramount bearing" on the restorative strategy.

Treatment planning — five phases

  1. Acute care — smooth a sharp cusp or incisal edge; desensitising agent or GIC over exposed dentine; pulp extirpation or, if severe, extraction; a provisional composite "bandage" for aesthetics; acute TMJ pain dysfunction from parafunction.
  2. Prevention.
  3. Stabilisation — caries control, active periodontal disease, oral mucosal lesions; extract hopeless teeth.
  4. Definitive restorations, including complex ones.
  5. Monitoring and maintenance. Review at each stage before moving to the next.

Prevention

  • Unlike caries, which affects most people, tooth wear has been seen as an individual rather than a community problem, and it is hard to predict who will be affected — so primary prevention is difficult.
  • Once diagnosed, wear usually progresses slowly (especially with preventive advice), but sporadic bursts occur with lifestyle changes — hence the need for a screening tool to detect and monitor wear over long periods.
  • Research has focused on erosion. Signs that erosion is quiescent: stain on previously affected surfaces (acid would remove it) and no dentine sensitivity.
MeasureDetails
1 · FluorideMany in vitro studies show benefit, but it has not been consistently confirmed clinically. Fluoride added to sports drinks reduced their erosive potential (Sorvari 1987). Topical F protects after an acid challenge, especially where dentine is exposed → daily neutral NaF rinse or gel. Avoid brushing soon after acid (e.g. vomiting); avoid low-pH mouthrinses. A remineralising toothpaste (Enamelon) hardened enamel more than conventional fluoride toothpaste.
2 · Desensitising0.7% fluoride solution in the surgery, then 0.4% stannous fluoride at home; potassium toothpastes; custom trays with reservoirs; Tooth Mousse (Recaldent — casein-derived; promotes remineralisation) in a modified bleaching tray.
3 · Diet and drinksCalcium lactate reduces the erosive potential of Coca-Cola; added citric acid (e.g. "twist of lime") increases it (in vitro); calcium-added Ribena Toothkind is less erosive. Reduce the amount and frequency of acidic food and drink and keep it to mealtimes; hard cheese or dairy afterwards helps enamel re-harden. Carbamide gum raises salivary pH rapidly; sugar-free, fluoride or carbamide gums stimulate saliva (TridentWhite contains Recaldent). Proflyin and Xerodent (with fluoride) promote salivation in xerostomia. TiF₄ and SnF₂ are under study and look promising.
4 · HabitsDrink acidic drinks through a wide-bore straw; don't swish; avoid overzealous brushing; use a less abrasive toothpaste; stop pen or pencil biting.
5 · SplintsConfirmed nocturnal bruxism → full-coverage hard acrylic splint (Michigan or Tanner) with an "ideal occlusion": even centric stops (at least one per opposing tooth), canine guidance (canine risers) separating the posterior teeth in excursions, and shared anterior guidance in protrusion (anterior ramp). Caution in reflux: acid can pool in the splint (bulimic patients may wear one while vomiting, with precise instructions). Soft vacuum-formed splints can have reservoirs for neutral fluoride gel or alkali (milk of magnesia, sodium bicarbonate).
6 · SealantsBonding agents or fissure sealant over eroded areas give some protection and reduce sensitivity; they are short-lived but may slow wear on treated surfaces for up to 9 months (Sundaram). GIC can be used the same way.
7 · Medical referralSuspected bulimia or reflux → GMP (antacids, omeprazole, ranitidine); xerostomia → oral medicine specialist.

Monitoring

  • The goal is to stop further pathological wear so that the rate returns to physiological. Early diagnosis plus effective prevention may be the definitive management. Avoid restorations where possible — they commit the patient to costly, long-term maintenance. Where restoration may be needed, first allow time to judge prevention (has the cause been removed? what is the rate of wear?).
  • Methods: high-quality sequential photographs; study casts every ~6–12 months (PVS impressions, vacuum-mixed die stone); a sectional silicone index from the first cast (hard to re-seat in generalised wear, which lacks stable reference points). These give only a gross, subjective estimate of the rate. Computer mapping of surface profiles is more precise but costly and impractical; indices are hard to apply routinely and vary between examiners.
  • Summary: most cases can be treated by passive, preventive measures with long-term monitoring and maintenance; a small proportion need active restoration.
Paper 2 · Loomans 2017 · European expert consensus

Severe tooth wear: European consensus statement on management guidelines

J Adhes Dent 2017;19(2):111–119 · 16 authors from the Netherlands, Switzerland, the UK, Germany and Denmark (including Mehta and Banerji) · corresponding author: Radboud University Medical Center, Nijmegen

Aims: critically appraise views and restorative options for severe tooth wear; give best-available-evidence guidance on when to start a programme of care and which approaches work best; identify gaps in knowledge.

Background

  • Erosive wear of permanent teeth affects about 30% of children and adolescents. Severe wear was found in 25% of 15-year-olds (El Aidi), and in 3% of 20-year-olds (with dentine exposure) vs 15% of 70-year-olds (Van't Spijker). In Dutch adults, mild to moderate wear is common and increases with age. Some patients belong to special risk groups, e.g. those with reflux symptoms.
  • Aetiology is usually multifactorial — erosion, abrasion and attrition. Severe wear may need complex care, possibly full rehabilitation at an increased vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO).
  • Treatment is shifting towards minimum-intervention approaches, which are less invasive but just as complex and demanding. Conventional approaches are still needed in some cases, but minimum intervention should be considered first.

Physiological or pathological?

  • Data on physiological wear are scarce: occlusal enamel wears about 15 µm/year on premolars and 29 µm/year on molars (Lambrechts). Incisor crowns shorten with age (Ray): maxillary from ~12 mm at age 10 to ~11 mm at 70 (~1 mm in six decades); mandibular from ~9.5 mm to 8 mm (~1.5 mm).
  • Ray found similar incisor wear in men and women, but most studies find more advanced wear in males.
  • Pathological wear is hard to quantify and define. The term describes unacceptable, progressive wear — usually ongoing wear severe enough to cause sensitivity, compromise appearance or cause functional problems.
  • Phasic activity: in a cohort of 70 people with severe wear followed for ≤12 months (Rodriguez), most progressed <15 µm, but some — particularly those with reflux symptoms — lost >100 µm in six months. Wear has periods of progression and remission, so prevention is appropriate at any stage, and a state-of-the-art diagnostic procedure is paramount.
  • Indices grade extent and severity, and serial scores showing progression can indicate a need for treatment. A single score is only a "snapshot" of a dynamic condition: a patient with the maximum score may not need, or suit, restoration at that time. Prevalence studies find a small group (2–10%, mostly young) with high levels of wear that could be called pathological, without concluding they should all be restored.

Severe or pathological?

TermConsensus definition
Severe tooth wear
— the amount lost (highest index grades)		Tooth wear with substantial loss of tooth structure, with dentine exposure and significant loss (≥⅓) of the clinical crown.
Pathological tooth wear
— active wear of atypical rate and nature		Tooth wear which is atypical for the age of the patient, causing pain or discomfort, functional problems, or deterioration of aesthetic appearance, which, if it progresses, may give rise to undesirable complications of increasing complexity.

A young patient with erosion, cupping in dentine and increased sensitivity can have pathological wear of limited severity; an 80-year-old can have severe wear that is not atypical for their age.

Risk assessment

  • Risk-assess the alternatives — including further prevention and monitoring only — bearing in mind further wear and the failure of restorations and prostheses. Episodes of wear may have different causes and rates.
  • Mechanical wear (attrition, abrasion) is enhanced by initial demineralisation (softening); hardly any loss is measurable without softening — hence the term "erosive tooth wear".
  • Diagnosis: quantify the wear, then identify the causes with a thorough oral history and validated questionnaires; OHIP-49 can measure oral-health-related quality of life. The multifactorial origin often prevents a clear diagnosis, and removing every cause may be unrealistic (long-standing chronic reflux, persistent bruxism).
  • Persistent bruxism (sleep and awake) limits the prognosis of brittle restorations (ceramic onlays, crowns); a persistently erosive environment limits partial-coverage restorations.
  • Every approach needs a robust preventive regime — e.g. a night-time occlusal splint (sleep bruxism), myofeedback therapy (awake bruxism), proton-pump inhibitors (gastric reflux).

To restore or not?

  • The amount of wear on an index should not be the major, let alone the only, basis for restoring.
  • Patient reasons: (1) sensitivity and/or pain; (2) difficulty chewing and eating; (3) impaired orofacial aesthetics; (4) "crumbling" of teeth and restorations. Or simple worry after wear is pointed out at a check-up.
  • Clinician — primary factors: (1) the amount of wear (grade); (2) the surfaces affected (involved in occlusion or articulation?); (3) the number of teeth (localised or generalised). Secondary factors: (1) progression (speed); (2) age; (3) aetiology.
  • Progression is judged from serial casts or digital 3D scans over months or years, which also help explain the condition to the patient. Progressive wear calls for preventive measures or referral (e.g. for gastric reflux) and reinforces compliance.
  • Decide jointly with the patient. No demands, concerns or symptoms → targeted prevention, counselling and monitoring. Clinically insignificant wear for age with no active wear → resist the patient's pleas for restorations. Benefits must clearly outweigh harms: never launch a patient into the "restorative death spiral" (Elderton) of failing restorations of ever-increasing complexity and cost.

The management protocol

  • Restoration is not always indicated. Advise prevention and arrange counselling and monitoring irrespective of severity.
  • If wear is progressing at a worrying rate, involve the patient in identifying the main causes and agree a preventive programme. Then:
    • No complaints → monitor the prevention with (digital) casts, intraoral images and an index. Once satisfied the wear isn't progressing, discuss whether restoration is needed; if monitoring continues, re-evaluate every 2 or 3 years.
    • Concerned about appearance or has complaints → critically review restorative options with the patient. No definitive restorations in the presence of active disease. Restorations (composites, full veneer crowns) don't prevent wear — they only change its rate, location and nature — and "definitive" restorations may have a limited lifetime with bruxism and erosion.
  • Conservative care can attract accusations of supervised neglect, so record patient engagement, severity (BEWE, TWI, TWES), shared decisions, actions taken and follow-up.

Restorative principles

  • Bruxism (fracture) or erosion plus bruxism (continued wear) can make restorations fail early, speeding up the restorative cycle — ever-larger restorations, more complications and eventually tooth loss. This matters most in young patients: minimum intervention may decide whether they have a functional, non-functional or no dentition in old age.
  • Postpone the first restoration — "once a restorative patient, always a restorative patient". Counselling and monitoring show how well prevention works, the rate of wear and the patient's compliance.
  • Take time to gather what is needed for robust informed consent: the patient must understand the risks and benefits of each option and have realistic expectations; document the process.
  • Restore "additively" rather than "subtractively": minimally invasive direct, indirect or hybrid techniques rather than very invasive traditional indirect restorations. This keeps future options open — the dynamic restorative concept (Creugers).
  • Traditional full and partial crowns are costly and carry a high risk of complications, some compromising the tooth — mainly a last resort (e.g. where composites keep failing, or in some older patients with cumulative disease and previous treatment).
  • Materials: no strong evidence that any one material is better (Mesko 2016 systematic review). Adhesive technique is critical: worn surfaces are dentine plus enamel, so use selective phosphoric-acid etching. Modern adhesives and hybrid composites can perform adequately; microfilled composites have high failure rates. Composites may need repair of fractures and chipping, especially in bruxists — say so at consent. Bruxists were excluded from crown and inlay studies, so the ~1–2% annual failure rates of controlled studies may not apply.
  • Increasing the VDO may be needed for function and aesthetics, to make space and to avoid removing sound tissue. A splint is rarely needed to test the increase, though a temporary splint may help planning and may be advisable with TMD.

The authors recommend three general principles (despite no high-level evidence):

  1. Restorations as conservative as possible, involving the minimum number of teeth.
  2. Preparation limited to necessary features — seats, bevels or chamfers — to aid placement.
  3. Assuming good oral hygiene, choose materials and technique by the patient's expectations, aesthetic demands and risk profile, operator familiarity and skills, availability for recall and budget.

Techniques

  • Localised severe wear — the Dahl concept (Dahl & Krogstad): axial tooth movement when an appliance or restorations are placed in supra-occlusion and full-arch contacts re-establish over time. Typically restorations on the palatal surfaces of the anterior teeth raise the VDO and, in time, create space for additive restorations. Over several months — possibly with condylar repositioning, compensatory eruption of the posterior teeth, some intrusion of the anteriors and alveolar remodelling — the posterior occlusion re-establishes at a new intercuspal position.
  • Generalised severe wear — direct composite: the DSO technique uses silicone stops to set the increased VDO and places composite directly; the mould and stamp techniques use a wax-up on casts to make a matrix for placing the composite.
  • Indirect: composite, ceramic or new polymer-ceramic CAD/CAM restorations, from conventional impressions and laboratory work to a fully digital workflow. Minimally invasive option: keep good-quality direct restorations and use indirect restorations for the occlusal part (a technique related to margin elevation).

Conclusion — the five guidelines

Restorative management of severe wear lacks a robust body of high-level evidence, and these patients' characteristics and higher failure risk mean existing restoration data cannot guide the choice of approach.

  1. Give priority to diagnosing the aetiology and instigating appropriate preventive measures.
  2. Moderate or severe wear without (functional or aesthetic) complaints → monitor first to see whether it is progressive.
  3. Restorative treatment should be as conservative as possible — minimally invasive, following a dynamic restorative concept.
  4. Use direct and indirect minimally invasive adhesive techniques; traditional invasive restorations remain an option in selected cases.
  5. Informed consent should explain the possible options and their expected complications.
