Strengths & limitations
Strengths
  • Mehta: a comprehensive, practical checklist (history, examination, special tests, indices, prevention, monitoring) illustrated with clinical photos; emphasises passive management; refereed CPD paper.
  • Loomans: multinational expert consensus; clear severe vs pathological definitions; a usable flowchart and five guidelines; patient-centred (shared decisions, consent, the death spiral); candid about evidence gaps.
Limitations
  • Mehta: narrative with no search method; much of the prevention evidence is in vitro (fluoride, drink modification) or from single studies; names commercial products; treats abfraction as a distinct type — a term a 2020 consensus (cited by Goodacre) discourages.
  • Loomans: expert opinion with no consensus method described; some recommended techniques (DSO, stamp) and the clinical examples come from the authors themselves; authors overlap with Mehta; little high-level restorative evidence (acknowledged).
  • Both: indices are snapshots that vary between examiners; no agreed norms of physiological wear for age; monitoring tools are imprecise (casts, photos) or costly (software).
Clinical relevance
  • Take a full history (reflux, vomiting, medications, a diet diary, brushing, habits, occupation) and record a baseline — index scores, photographs, casts or scans.
  • Prevention and monitoring come first, whatever the severity; refer suspected reflux or eating disorders.
  • Restore only for patient complaints or clinician concern once wear is controlled — additively and minimally invasively (e.g. Dahl palatal composites, direct composite at an increased VDO) — with documented informed consent.
Exam practice
SAQDistinguish "severe" from "pathological" tooth wear (Loomans 2017).

Severe = substantial loss of tooth structure with dentine exposure and loss of ≥⅓ of the clinical crown — an amount (the highest index grades). Pathological = wear atypical for the patient's age causing pain or discomfort, functional problems or aesthetic deterioration, which may lead to complications if it progresses — active wear of atypical rate and nature. A young patient with erosive cupping and sensitivity can have pathological wear of limited severity; an 80-year-old can have severe wear that is not atypical for their age.

SAQDescribe the clinical features of erosion and how extrinsic and intrinsic erosion differ in distribution.

Bilateral concave defects without the chalkiness of caries: early, a shallow, smooth, glazed, plaque-free surface lacking developmental ridges and stain lines; later dull exposed dentine and cupping of occlusal surfaces and incisal edges. Extrinsic (dietary) → scooped-out depressions on the labial surfaces of maxillary anteriors. Intrinsic (gastric) → the whole palatal surface of the maxillary anteriors ("perimolysis" with chronic vomiting). The tongue holds acid against the upper palatal surfaces, while the lower anteriors are bathed in submandibular and sublingual saliva.

SAQList the Turner & Missirlian categories of generalised wear and explain the role of dento-alveolar compensation.

(1) Excessive wear with loss of OVD; (2) excessive wear without loss of OVD, but with space available; (3) excessive wear without loss of OVD, but with limited space. Slow wear with secondary supra-eruption of the dento-alveolar processes maintains the OVD and is thought to explain categories 2 and 3. The category shapes the restorative strategy — in category 3 there is little room for restorative material.

SAQGive five preventive measures for a patient with erosive wear (Mehta 2012).

Reduce the amount and frequency of acidic food and drink and keep it to mealtimes; finish with hard cheese or dairy; use a wide-bore straw and don't swish; don't brush soon after acid or vomiting, and use a less abrasive paste; daily neutral NaF rinse or gel ± Tooth Mousse; sugar-free or carbamide gum to stimulate saliva; a splint with reservoirs for fluoride gel; bonding agent or sealant over eroded areas; refer suspected reflux or bulimia to the GMP.

SAQCompare the TWI and the BEWE.

TWI (Smith & Knight): grades 0–4, from loss of enamel surface characteristics to pulp or secondary-dentine exposure; the most popular index, used to compare individuals and monitor progression, but it doesn't relate aetiology to outcome. BEWE (Bartlett 2010): modelled on the BPE — the worst tooth in each sextant scored 0–3 (no wear; initial loss of surface texture; <50%; >50% surface loss), summed to an aggregate score that guides management; simple to use, but its sensitivity and specificity need study.

SAQExplain the Dahl concept.

For localised wear without space: restorations (typically palatal composites on the anterior teeth) or an appliance are placed in supra-occlusion, so the posterior teeth are apart. Over several months the posterior teeth erupt, the anteriors intrude, the alveolar bone remodels (± condylar repositioning) and full-arch contact returns at a new intercuspal position — creating space for additive restorations without removing tooth tissue.

SAQWhat is the "restorative death spiral", and how does Loomans suggest avoiding it?

The cycle in which restorations fail (fracture from bruxism, continued wear from erosion and bruxism) and are replaced by ever-larger, costlier restorations with more complications, eventually leading to tooth loss (Elderton) — most important in young patients. Avoid it by prevention and monitoring first, postponing the first restoration, placing no definitive restorations during active wear, using additive minimally invasive techniques (the dynamic restorative concept), and deciding jointly with full informed consent.

LAQA 24-year-old presents with sensitive, "shorter" upper front teeth. Discuss your assessment and management, using Mehta 2012 and Loomans 2017.
  1. History: chief complaint; medical (reflux, eating disorders, asthma, medications); a 3-day diet diary (acidic drinks — frequency, method, timing); brushing; habits and bruxism; occupation and sport.
  2. Examination and tests: extra-oral (parotids, TMJ, freeway space); the pattern of wear — palatal maxillary (intrinsic) vs labial (extrinsic), cupping, facets; TWI, BEWE or ACE scores; occlusion (CR→CO slide, space); sensibility tests; photographs, articulated casts or scans; saliva.
  3. Diagnosis: erosive wear ± attrition, localised anterior; likely pathological but not yet severe; is it active (sensitivity, no stain)?
  4. Management: acute care (desensitise, cover exposed dentine) → prevention (diet, straw, timing of brushing, neutral fluoride, Tooth Mousse; refer suspected reflux or bulimia) → monitor progression (casts every 6–12 months, or scans) → if wear progresses or concerns the patient, a shared decision on additive restoration (e.g. palatal composites with Dahl; ACE II–III) with informed consent and full records → maintenance. Avoid starting the death spiral in a young patient.
  5. Evidence: both papers are narrative or consensus; there is little high-level restorative evidence.
